plain_summary: This bill proposes to abolish business rates, which is a yearly tax based on the estimated rental value of non-residential buildings like shops and offices. If passed, businesses would no longer pay this tax, but the government would need to find another way to replace the lost money.

This bill would modify the current abortion law in England and Wales. It aims to prevent abortions being carried out solely because the unborn baby is expected to have a disability, treating disability as equal to non-disability in the eyes of the law. The bill is controversial because it affects a woman's right to choose and doctors' ability to provide medical advice.

This bill would make it a criminal offense for doctors to knowingly perform an abortion when the main reason is the sex of the unborn baby. It aims to prevent sex-selective abortion, which some people believe happens in certain communities.

This bill reforms absent voting procedures for elections held in Scotland and Wales, making it easier for eligible voters to cast ballots when they cannot attend polling stations in person. The legislation likely expands access to postal votes, proxy votes, or early in-person voting options, and may streamline the application process or extend eligibility criteria. These changes aim to increase voter participation and accommodate people with work commitments, disabilities, caring responsibilities, or those living away from their registered address during election periods.

The Academies Act 2010 allows schools to become 'academies' - schools run independently from local councils but still funded by the government. These schools have more freedom to make their own decisions about what they teach, how they spend money, and who they employ, instead of following council rules.

This bill asks Parliament to create and publish a report examining the Access to Elected Office Fund - a scheme designed to help people who couldn't otherwise afford to stand for election. The report would look at how well the fund is working and whether it's actually helping people from poorer backgrounds become MPs or councillors.

This bill aims to improve female entrepreneurs' access to business finance by introducing measures to address the well-documented funding gap between male and female-led businesses. The legislation likely includes requirements for lenders and financial institutions to report on their lending practices to women-owned businesses, potentially mandating diversity targets or enhanced support schemes. It may also establish government-backed loan guarantees or grants specifically for women entrepreneurs, and require banks to provide tailored financial advice and mentoring. The bill seeks to remove structural barriers that have historically resulted in women receiving smaller loans and facing higher rejection rates compared to male applicants.

This bill aims to make palliative care (treatment that focuses on comfort rather than cure) more available and accessible to children across the UK who have life-limiting or life-threatening illnesses. It seeks to ensure these children and their families can get the support and pain relief they need without unnecessary delays or barriers.

This bill aims to give adoptive parents fairer treatment when they take time off work to care for their new children. It would provide statutory leave, pay during that leave, and allowances for adoptive parents - bringing their entitlements closer to those given to parents who have biological children.

This Act creates ARIA, a new government agency designed to fund ambitious, high-risk scientific research projects that might not get traditional funding. It operates with more freedom than typical government bodies, aiming to speed up innovation in areas like technology, medicine, and engineering.

This bill aims to make it easier and cheaper for UK citizens to buy their own homes. It would introduce measures to help people overcome barriers like saving for a large deposit or getting a mortgage, particularly targeting first-time buyers and lower-income households.

This bill aims to create consistent rules for how online platforms verify users' ages to prevent children accessing age-restricted content and services. It would require websites and apps to use reliable age-assurance methods (like ID checks or other verification), rather than just asking 'Are you over 18?' with no verification.

This bill would change the age at which young people can be charged and tried as criminals in the UK. It aims to treat younger children differently in the justice system, potentially moving them away from adult courts and towards more educational or rehabilitation-focused approaches instead.

This bill aims to address Age-Related Macular Degeneration, an eye condition affecting older people that can lead to blindness. It would probably improve how the NHS treats, diagnoses, or supports patients with AMD, though the exact details aren't fully clear at this stage.

The Agricultural Land (Planning) Bill modifies planning regulations to affect how agricultural land can be developed or protected in the UK. It likely adjusts the rules governing when farmers can build on their land, how planning permission is assessed for agricultural projects, or what protections exist for productive farmland. The bill aims to balance agricultural productivity, rural development needs, and environmental considerations through changes to the planning system. Specific measures would determine whether this makes it easier or harder to develop agricultural land for non-farming purposes.

This bill aims to control alcohol advertising to make it less attractive and accessible to young people. It would introduce new rules about where alcohol ads can appear (like on TV, online, or billboards) and how they can be designed, with the goal of protecting children's health and reducing alcohol-related problems.

This Act is a specific law dealing with Allhallows Staining Church in the City of London. It sets out rules for how the church should be managed, looked after, and governed, protecting the building as a historic monument and ensuring its long-term care.

This bill introduces a mandatory licensing system for animal shelters across the UK, requiring facilities to meet set standards before operating legally. Shelters would need to demonstrate compliance with animal welfare requirements, staffing qualifications, and operational practices verified through regular inspections. The system aims to prevent substandard facilities from operating and protect animals in care by establishing consistent, enforceable minimum standards. Local authorities or a designated regulator would oversee licensing, with powers to refuse or revoke licenses for non-compliance.

This bill introduces stricter controls on importing dogs, cats, and ferrets into the UK to protect animal welfare and public health. It requires pets to meet specific health and vaccination standards before entry, restricts imports from high-risk countries, and aims to crack down on illegal puppy smuggling. The legislation replaces previous EU regulations that no longer apply post-Brexit and establishes new UK-specific import rules enforced by animal health officials.

This bill establishes clear legal responsibility for dog owners whose dogs attack other dogs. It aims to clarify liability, compensation, and potentially criminal accountability when a dog injures or kills another person's dog. The bill would likely create a framework for determining fault, enforcing financial compensation for veterinary costs and losses, and may introduce penalties for owners who fail to control their animals. This addresses a current legal grey area where victims of dog-on-dog attacks often struggle to obtain justice or compensation.

This bill would give arrested people anonymity - meaning their names, faces, and details would not be revealed to the public or media until they are officially charged with a crime. Currently, police can name arrested people straight away, but this bill would change that.

This bill aims to create rules for 'anti-loitering devices', gadgets that emit sounds or signals designed to discourage young people from gathering in certain areas. The bill would regulate how, where, and when these devices can be used to balance public safety concerns with protecting people's rights and wellbeing.

The Anti-Slavery Day Act 2010 establishes a national day (18 October) dedicated to raising awareness about slavery and human trafficking. It encourages people and organizations to think about modern slavery and take steps to prevent it, helping to protect people who are exploited or forced to work.

This Act gives police and councils stronger powers to deal with anti-social behaviour, things like loud parties, harassment, or aggressive behaviour in public spaces. It lets authorities issue quick orders to stop problem behaviour and includes stricter punishments, but it also removes some traditional legal protections that people usually have.

This bill aims to acknowledge that many people feel serious anxiety and worry about environmental issues, and proposes that the government should do something about it. It's essentially asking Parliament to recognize 'eco-anxiety' as an important problem and take steps to address the concerns behind it.

This Act is designed to reform apprenticeships, making them more available and high-quality for people wanting to learn trades and skills. It also aims to improve how children are taught in schools and ensure young people leave education better prepared for work.

This Act gives the government official permission to spend money from the public budget on various government services and departments for that year. It's essentially Parliament saying 'yes, the government can now pay for these things' - without it, the government couldn't legally spend taxpayers' money.

The Arbitration Act 2025 updates UK law to modernise how disputes between businesses and individuals are resolved outside of courts through arbitration. The Act streamlines arbitration procedures, clarifies the powers of arbitrators, and establishes new rules for managing complex commercial disputes more efficiently. It aims to make arbitration faster and more cost-effective than traditional court proceedings while maintaining fairness and due process. The legislation reflects international best practices and positions the UK as a competitive centre for international dispute resolution.

This bill extends equality laws to arbitration and mediation services. Currently, these private dispute-settling services aren't fully covered by equality legislation, so this bill would make them follow the same non-discrimination rules as shops, employers, and other businesses.

This bill aims to make sure that private arbitration and mediation services (which help people and businesses settle disagreements without going to court) cannot discriminate against people and must treat everyone fairly. Currently, there's uncertainty about whether equality laws fully apply to these services, so the bill would make it clear they must follow the same non-discrimination rules as other businesses.

This bill aims to ensure that private arbitration and mediation services follow the same equality and non-discrimination laws that apply to other UK businesses. Currently, these dispute-resolution services may not be fully covered by equality laws, so this bill would close that gap and protect people from unfair treatment.

This bill ensures that private arbitration and mediation services (alternatives to going to court to resolve disagreements) must follow UK equality laws. Currently, these services may not be covered by the same anti-discrimination protections that apply to courts, so this bill aims to close that gap and protect people from unfair treatment based on their personal characteristics.

This bill aims to give Parliament more power to hold arm's-length bodies accountable. These are public organizations like health agencies or cultural institutions that operate semi-independently from government, the bill would strengthen Parliament's ability to question them and ensure they're answering to elected representatives.

The Arm's-Length Bodies (Review) Bill establishes a formal process for the government to review and potentially restructure or abolish public bodies that operate independently from direct ministerial control, such as quangos, regulators, and executive agencies. The bill gives ministers powers to examine whether these bodies remain necessary, efficient, and aligned with government objectives, potentially consolidating or eliminating duplicative organizations. It aims to reduce bureaucratic complexity and redirect public funding more effectively, though it also centralizes control over institutions designed to operate at arm's length from political influence.

The Armed Conflict (Requirements) Bill establishes formal parliamentary requirements that must be met before the UK can engage in armed military action abroad. The bill seeks to place legal obligations on the government to seek parliamentary approval before committing armed forces to conflict, with limited exceptions for emergency self-defence. This would codify into law what has been largely a political convention since the 2003 Iraq War vote. The legislation aims to strengthen parliamentary scrutiny and democratic accountability over decisions to deploy military force.

This Act gives members of the armed forces (army, navy, air force) the legal right to request flexible working arrangements, such as part-time hours or adjusted schedules. It brings military personnel in line with civilian workers' rights to balance work and personal life, though requests can still be refused if they would harm military operations.

This bill aims to prevent discrimination in the UK Armed Forces by making anti-discrimination laws clearer and more comprehensive. It would ensure that all service members are treated fairly and have proper legal recourse if they face unfair treatment because of who they are.

This bill updates the laws that control the Volunteer Reserve - people who serve part-time in the British Armed Forces alongside their regular jobs. It aims to modernize how these reservists work and are supported by the military.

This bill asks the UK Parliament to officially declare that the deaths of Armenians between 1915-1923, when the Ottoman Empire controlled the region, was genocide, meaning it was deliberately planned mass killing of a particular group of people. Currently, the UK has not made an official statement on this, though many countries including France and Germany have.

This bill asks the UK Parliament to officially recognise and acknowledge that the mass killing of around 1.5 million Armenian people between 1915-1923 was genocide. Currently, the UK government hasn't made an official statement on this, though many other countries and historians say it was genocide. The bill would change this by making Parliament's position clear.

This bill establishes a formal inquiry mechanism into UK arms exports and creates powers to suspend arms sales to specific countries. It would require the government to investigate whether exported weapons are being used in violation of international humanitarian law or human rights conventions. If the inquiry finds evidence of misuse, the government would gain statutory authority to temporarily halt arms sales to the affected country without requiring new parliamentary legislation each time. The bill aims to provide a faster, more systematic process for reviewing arms sales rather than relying on ad-hoc political decisions.

This bill aims to increase parliamentary oversight of arm's-length bodies, organisations like NHS trusts, public agencies, and quangos that operate independently but are funded by or accountable to government departments. The bill would require these bodies to provide regular reports to Parliament, establish clearer accountability mechanisms, and give MPs greater powers to scrutinise their decisions and spending. The measures seek to close gaps where public money is spent by organisations that currently have limited direct accountability to elected representatives.

The Artificial Intelligence (Regulation) Bill establishes a regulatory framework for AI systems used in the UK, requiring developers and deployers to assess and manage risks before releasing AI into the market. The bill creates oversight mechanisms to ensure high-risk AI applications, such as those used in recruitment, law enforcement, or critical infrastructure, meet safety and transparency standards. It grants regulators powers to investigate breaches, issue fines, and require companies to modify or withdraw harmful AI systems. The legislation aims to balance innovation with public protection by setting binding requirements rather than purely voluntary guidelines.

This bill would require the government to regularly assess and report on how its policies impact families - such as laws about taxes, benefits, education, or health. It's designed to make sure politicians think carefully about family life before creating new policies, and to be transparent about the effects these policies will have.

This bill would allow terminally ill adults in England and Wales to request medical assistance to end their life. To qualify, a person must be diagnosed with a condition expected to cause death within six months, be mentally competent to make the decision, and go through a formal process involving two doctors' assessments and a court application. If approved, a doctor could then prescribe medication that the person self-administers. The bill creates strict safeguards including waiting periods and multiple medical checks to prevent coercion or hasty decisions.

This Act sets out the legal rules for electric vehicles and self-driving cars in the UK. It clarifies who is responsible when these vehicles cause accidents (usually the insurer), defines what counts as an 'automated vehicle,' and makes sure people injured by these cars can claim compensation fairly.

This bill aims to make it a requirement (or at least strongly encourage) councils and public organisations to install Automated External Defibrillators in accessible public places. The goal is to have these life-saving machines readily available so that anyone can use them to help someone experiencing sudden cardiac arrest while waiting for emergency services to arrive.

This Act creates rules and safety standards for self-driving vehicles in the UK. It allows companies to test and use cars that can drive themselves without a human controlling them, while setting up a legal framework for who is responsible if something goes wrong.

This bill proposes to change the autumn bank holiday - the day in late August/early September when most UK workers get a day off. The exact change isn't clear from the title alone, but it would alter when this holiday is celebrated or how it works.

The Aviation (Accessibility) Bill aims to improve access to air travel for disabled passengers and those with mobility challenges. It sets enforceable standards for UK airports and airlines regarding facilities, assistance, and services, such as wheelchair accessibility, trained staff support, and accessible toilets and seating. The bill creates legal obligations for aviation operators to meet these standards and establishes mechanisms for complaints and enforcement. This legislation ensures disabled travellers have comparable experiences to non-disabled passengers when using UK airports and flights.

This bill aims to combat financial exclusion by requiring banks to maintain basic banking services for all customers and preventing arbitrary account closures. It establishes minimum standards for access to essential banking facilities such as current accounts, payment services, and cash withdrawal options, particularly for vulnerable groups. The bill also creates obligations for banks to provide transparent reasons when refusing or terminating customer relationships, and establishes an appeals process. These measures seek to address the growing problem of people being locked out of the financial system, which can lead to reliance on high-cost lending and exclusion from employment and services.

This bill proposes replacing the Barnett Formula, a 40-year-old method that calculates how much government funding Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland receive based on England's spending. The bill would create a new way to distribute money that the supporters believe would be more fair and up-to-date.

This bill proposes replacing the Barnett Formula, a 40-year-old system that allocates government funding to Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, with a new method. The bill aims to create a fairer way of distributing UK government money between different parts of the country based on their actual needs.

This bill establishes mandatory fire safety standards and regulations for Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) - large-scale installations that store electrical energy in batteries, increasingly used to support the UK's renewable energy transition. The legislation requires operators to implement specific safety measures, fire detection and suppression systems, and maintain minimum distances from residential areas and critical infrastructure. It aims to prevent incidents like the Kilroot battery storage fire in Northern Ireland (2023) and similar events that have caused environmental damage and safety risks. The bill creates enforcement mechanisms and penalties for non-compliance with these safety requirements.

This bill proposes to abolish the BBC licence fee - the annual charge that UK households currently pay to watch or record live TV on any channel, or to use BBC iPlayer. The money from these fees currently pays for BBC services like television, radio, and online content. The bill would end this system entirely.

This bill would allow the BBC to issue financial penalties directly to people who refuse to pay their TV licence fee, without having to take them to criminal court. Currently, the BBC can only prosecute non-payers through the legal system; this would give them a faster, simpler way to enforce payment.

This bill would change the law so that people aged 75 and over cannot be prosecuted criminally (taken to court as a crime) if they don't pay their BBC licence fee. Currently, anyone who doesn't pay can face criminal charges; this bill would remove that punishment for over-75s only, though they could still receive a fine instead.

This bill would stop over-75s from being prosecuted (taken to court) and potentially given a criminal record for not paying their BBC licence fee. Instead, they would face civil action like a fine, similar to other money disputes. It's intended to protect elderly people from serious criminal consequences.

This bill would remove the threat of criminal charges against people aged 75 and over who don't pay their BBC television licence fee. Currently, non-payment can lead to court cases and fines; this bill would stop that happening specifically for older people in this age group.

This bill removes the criminal penalties for non-payment of BBC television licence fees specifically for people aged 75 and over. Currently, failure to pay the licence fee can result in prosecution and criminal conviction, with potential fines up to £1,000. Under this bill, over-75s who don't pay would no longer face criminal charges, though civil enforcement mechanisms might still apply. The measure aims to prevent elderly people from entering the criminal justice system due to licence fee debt.

This bill would change the BBC from a publicly-owned broadcaster (funded by TV licence fees paid by viewers) into a private company or companies that operate for profit. It represents a major shift in how British broadcasting is organised and funded.

This bill proposes changing the BBC from a publicly-owned broadcaster (funded by TV licences) into a private company that would need to make its own money through advertising and subscriptions. It would fundamentally change how the BBC operates and is paid for.

This bill would transform the BBC from a state-owned broadcaster funded by TV licences into a private company. It would fundamentally change how the BBC operates, is funded, and serves the British public.

This bill aims to improve bereavement support services specifically for children and young people who have experienced the death of a parent, sibling, or other close person. It likely establishes or strengthens access to counselling, mental health services, and practical support through schools, NHS services, and community organisations. The bill recognises that children and young people have distinct bereavement needs that differ from adults and require tailored, age-appropriate interventions. The measures probably include funding commitments, training requirements for professionals, and coordination between education and health services.

This bill would change the rules around gaming machines in betting shops. Category B2 machines are mid-level gaming terminals that allow people to gamble money. The bill would likely allow betting shops to have more of these machines, which they currently cannot do under existing regulations.

This Act protects the traditional rights and privileges of Beverley Freemen - a group with historical status in Beverley, East Yorkshire. It ensures they keep their long-established freedoms, which typically include things like the right to graze animals on common land or trade without certain restrictions.

This bill proposes to legally require children to wear safety helmets when riding bicycles. It aims to protect young cyclists from serious injury by making helmet-wearing a requirement rather than just a recommendation.

This bill would allow juries in Wales to use the Welsh language during court cases. Currently, jury trials in Wales must be conducted in English. The bill would give Welsh speakers the option to use their language, making the courts more inclusive for Welsh-speaking people in Wales.

The Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction Act 2026 enables the UK to ratify and implement an international agreement protecting marine life in ocean areas beyond any nation's control (international waters covering about half the world's oceans). The bill creates legal mechanisms for the UK to participate in a global framework that establishes marine protected areas, requires environmental impact assessments for ocean activities, and enables benefit-sharing from marine genetic resources. It effectively gives the UK a voice in governing and conserving the high seas while committing to enforceable conservation standards.

The Borders, Citizenship and Immigration Act 2009 reformed UK immigration law by introducing a points-based system to manage skilled migration, strengthening border controls, and changing citizenship requirements. It gave the UK Border Agency enhanced powers to enforce immigration rules, introduced biometric technology for identity verification, and made it harder to obtain British citizenship by increasing residency requirements and introducing citizenship tests. The Act aimed to create a more selective immigration system that prioritises skilled workers while maintaining stricter security and identity controls.

The Breast Cancer Screening (Review) Bill requires the government to conduct a comprehensive review of the NHS breast cancer screening programme, examining its current effectiveness, scope, and delivery. The review would assess whether screening guidelines (particularly age ranges and frequency) remain evidence-based and whether the programme is reaching all eligible women equitably. The bill aims to ensure screening recommendations reflect the latest medical research and address any gaps in access or uptake across different communities.

This bill would change NHS policy to make breast cancer screening available to women under 40. Currently, the NHS mainly screens women aged 50-74, so this bill would extend that programme to include younger women.

This bill focuses on breast cancer screening - the regular checks that help detect breast cancer early in women. It likely aims to improve, expand, or change how these screening services are delivered across the UK's NHS.

This bill proposes to privatise the BBC, selling it from public ownership to private owners rather than keeping it as a publicly-funded service. Currently, the BBC is funded by TV licence fees paid by UK households. Under privatisation, it would operate as a private company, likely funded differently, such as through subscriptions or advertising.

This bill proposes to privatise the BBC - changing it from a public service funded by TV licence fees into a private company. Currently, the BBC is owned by the public and funded by mandatory TV licence payments; this bill would end that arrangement and allow private ownership instead.

This bill would end the BBC's status as a publicly-owned broadcaster and turn it into a private company or companies instead. Currently, the BBC is funded by TV licence fees paid by households and operates as a public service; this bill would change that system entirely.

This bill would end the BBC's status as a publicly-owned broadcaster and convert it into a privately-owned company. The government would sell the BBC to private investors or a commercial operator, replacing the current licence fee system (where UK households pay an annual charge) with a different funding model. The bill fundamentally changes how the BBC operates, from a public service accountable to Parliament to a private enterprise accountable to shareholders.

This bill aims to help British victims of terrorism get financial compensation by allowing the government to freeze money and assets belonging to terrorists or terror-linked groups, then use that money to pay victims. It's designed to make sure terrorists' wealth can't be kept and used, while helping those who have suffered from attacks.

The British-Made Bricks (Proposals) Bill would establish new measures to support and promote the production of bricks manufactured within the United Kingdom. The bill likely includes provisions to define what qualifies as 'British-made,' set standards for domestic brick production, and potentially provide incentives or preferential treatment for British brick manufacturers in public procurement. It aims to strengthen the domestic brick industry and reduce reliance on imported bricks for construction projects.

This bill keeps certain major sporting events on free-to-watch TV channels in the UK rather than allowing them to be shown only on paid subscription services. It creates a 'listed events' system so that famous competitions must include free coverage that all UK households can access, even if other channels also show the full event on subscription platforms.

This bill would abolish the television licence fee - the annual charge that UK households must currently pay to watch live TV or use BBC iPlayer. Instead of this system, the BBC and other broadcasters would need to find different ways to pay for their services, such as advertising or subscription fees.

This bill would abolish the television licence fee - the annual charge that UK households must pay to watch live TV and access BBC services. Instead of the current system where everyone pays a fee, the BBC would need to find other ways to fund itself, such as through subscriptions or government grants.

The Budget Responsibility Act 2024 establishes stronger mechanisms for monitoring government spending and requiring Parliament to review long-term fiscal sustainability. The bill aims to create independent oversight of budget forecasts and spending plans, potentially including new reporting requirements on public debt trajectories. It seeks to ensure greater transparency around how government finances are managed and to prevent unsustainable spending commitments that could burden future generations. The legislation reflects concerns about maintaining fiscal discipline while managing competing demands for public services.

This bill asks the government to carry out a formal review of the Building Regulations - the set of rules that builders and architects must follow when constructing buildings. The review will look at whether these regulations are still fit for purpose and whether they need updating for modern times.

The Building Safety Act 2022 introduces tougher safety standards and oversight for high-rise residential buildings in England. It requires better quality control during construction, regular inspections, and clearer responsibility for keeping buildings safe, particularly in response to fires like the Grenfell Tower tragedy.

This bill proposes to set maximum working hours for bus drivers who work on local routes (buses that stop regularly in towns and cities, rather than long-distance coaches). It aims to protect drivers' health and wellbeing by preventing them from working excessive hours.

This bill aims to require buses in the UK to become zero-emission vehicles, likely electric. It's designed to reduce air pollution from buses, which are used by millions of people daily, and help the UK meet its climate change goals.

The Business and Planning Act 2020 is a temporary law that relaxes rules for businesses to use public outdoor spaces (like streets and pavements) for things like outdoor seating and serving food and drink. It was designed to help shops, cafes and restaurants operate during and after the COVID-19 pandemic by removing bureaucratic obstacles.

This bill proposes creating a new 'Business of the House Commission' - a committee that would help organize and manage how Parliament conducts its business, such as planning debate schedules and coordinating parliamentary activities. It's designed to make Parliament more efficient and better organized.

This bill requires the government to report to Parliament regularly about cancer research funding - how much money is being spent, where it's going, and what progress is being made. It's designed to make cancer research funding more transparent and accountable to MPs and taxpayers.

This bill gives the government and local councils new powers to regulate caravan sites - including where they can be built and how they're managed. It affects both permanent caravan residents and travelling communities who live in caravans.

This bill changes the laws controlling caravan sites across the UK. It likely deals with things like safety standards, how sites should be managed, residents' rights, or planning rules - but without more details about the specific proposals, the exact impact isn't clear from the title alone.

This bill sets legally binding targets to reduce carbon emissions from buildings in the UK, requiring the construction and property sector to achieve net zero emissions by a specified date. It establishes requirements for new buildings to meet strict energy efficiency standards and places obligations on owners of existing buildings to retrofit them with low-carbon heating systems, improved insulation, and renewable energy sources. The bill creates enforcement mechanisms and reporting requirements to track progress toward these targets, with financial penalties for non-compliance. It aims to decarbonise buildings, which account for approximately 25% of UK carbon emissions.

This bill aims to create an official identification system for carers - people who look after elderly relatives, disabled family members, or seriously ill friends without being paid. The ID would help carers prove their status to get access to benefits, discounts, and services designed to support them.

This bill requires ceramic products (like plates, bowls, and pottery) sold in the UK to have a clear label showing where they were made. It aims to help shoppers know if they're buying British-made ceramics or imports, and to support the UK ceramic industry.

This Act makes changes to the rules and powers around the Channel Tunnel Rail Link rail project. It adjusts legal arrangements and gives authorities additional powers needed to complete and manage the high-speed rail connection between London and the Channel Tunnel.

This bill updates the laws about cheques in the UK. Cheques are old-fashioned payment methods, and the bill probably changes how banks handle them, who can use them, or how long they're valid for. The changes aim to reflect how payment methods have modernised.

This bill would require the UK government to set a legal target for reducing child poverty and regularly report on whether they're meeting it. It aims to make tackling child poverty a legal requirement rather than just an optional goal, forcing lawmakers to take measurable action to help children in low-income families.

This bill proposes to remove the two-child limit from the Universal Credit and Child Tax Credit systems, which currently restricts benefit payments to the first two children in a household. Under current rules, families receive no additional support from these benefits for a third child or beyond, regardless of financial need. If passed, the bill would allow all children in a household to qualify for their full entitlement to these benefits. The measure aims to reduce child poverty by increasing financial support to larger families.

This Act strengthens the rules and powers used to make parents pay child support they legally owe. It gives authorities better tools to collect payments from parents who aren't paying, including potentially stronger penalties for non-payment, to ensure children get financial support from both their parents.

The Childcare Act 2016 provides government-funded free childcare hours for eligible young children in England. It aims to help working parents afford childcare by offering 30 hours per week of free care for children aged 3-4, making it easier for parents to balance work and family life.

The Childcare Payments Act 2014 allows the government to offer financial help to working parents to pay for childcare. It does this through tax-free childcare accounts where parents can save money to spend on approved childcare, reducing the cost of looking after their children while they work.

This bill aims to make the law clearer about who is responsible for looking after children who are in the care system (rather than with their parents). It would set out better rules about custody and decision-making to protect these vulnerable children and make sure they're properly cared for.

The Children's Hospices (Funding) Bill establishes a dedicated, sustainable funding mechanism for children's hospices across the UK. These services provide specialist care for children with life-limiting conditions and support for their families. The bill likely commits government funding to ensure hospices can maintain and expand services without relying solely on charitable donations. This addresses a significant gap in healthcare provision for some of the most vulnerable children and their families.

This bill aims to set up 'Citizens' Conventions' - groups of randomly selected members of the public who would meet to discuss and debate important policy issues, then provide recommendations to Parliament. It's designed to give ordinary people a direct say in how the country is run, beyond just voting in elections.

This bill would allow Civil Enforcement Officers (who handle parking and other civil breaches) and Traffic Wardens (who manage traffic flow and parking) to have their roles combined into one position in England. The aim is to make local enforcement simpler and potentially more cost-effective by having fewer separate job types.

The Civil Liability Act 2018 changes the rules for personal injury claims (like car accident or slip-and-fall cases) in UK courts. It makes it tougher to win compensation by increasing the threshold of injury needed to claim, and it reduces the amounts people can receive, particularly for whiplash injuries.

This bill proposes to make changes to the Civil Partnership Act 2004, which is the law that allows same-sex couples to have their relationships legally recognized. The bill is at the 2nd reading stage, where MPs debate whether the proposed changes are a good idea before voting on them.

This bill proposes to update the Civil Partnership Act 2004, which is the law that lets same-sex couples (and now different-sex couples) enter into a legal partnership similar to marriage. The amendment would change some of the rules around civil partnerships, though the exact changes aren't specified in this basic information.

This bill proposes changes to the Civil Partnership Act 2004, which is the law that lets same-sex couples form official legal partnerships with similar rights to marriage. The amendment would modify parts of this law, though the specific details of the changes would become clearer as the bill progresses through Parliament.

This bill would change the law to allow opposite-sex couples to enter into civil partnerships, which currently are only available to same-sex couples. Civil partnerships provide similar legal rights and responsibilities to marriage but are a different legal status. The bill essentially extends this option to everyone, not just same-sex couples.

This Act updates and modernises the laws about how civil partnerships (legal unions for same-sex couples), marriages, and deaths are officially registered in the UK. It makes changes to the registration process to reflect modern practices and hopefully simplify the system for ordinary people.

This bill aims to set up a 'Code of Practice' - a set of official guidelines that companies must follow when removing or replacing dangerous cladding from buildings. Cladding is the outer material on buildings, and some types are unsafe, so this bill would make sure the repair work is done to a proper standard.

This bill amends the Clean Neighbourhoods and Environment Act 2005 to strengthen local authorities' powers to tackle environmental crime and anti-social behaviour. It introduces new enforcement measures allowing councils to issue fixed penalties for littering, fly-posting, and graffiti offences, and expands their ability to prosecute environmental violations more efficiently. The amendments aim to improve local environmental standards and give councils more tools to maintain cleaner public spaces without requiring full court proceedings for minor offences.

The Climate and Nature Bill is legislation designed to strengthen the UK's legal framework for meeting climate targets and protecting biodiversity. It establishes binding commitments to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to net-zero by 2050 and sets intermediate targets for 2030 and 2035. The bill also requires the government to implement nature recovery programmes, restore habitats, and monitor environmental outcomes through new enforcement mechanisms and statutory duties on public bodies.

The Climate Change Act 2008 is a law that requires the UK government to cut greenhouse gas emissions (pollution that causes global warming) by at least 80% by 2050. It sets five-year targets to track progress and creates an independent committee to advise the government on whether it's meeting its climate goals.

This bill would establish a dedicated Climate Finance Fund to redirect money away from fossil fuel subsidies and pollution-related spending toward climate action and clean energy investment. The fund would be financed by removing or reducing government financial support for oil, gas, and coal industries, and by reallocating money currently spent managing pollution-related health and environmental costs. The bill aims to accelerate the UK's transition to renewable energy while reducing the hidden costs of fossil fuel dependence on the NHS, environment, and economy.

This bill aims to increase the use of CCTV cameras in the UK and promote their installation in public and private spaces. It would give the government powers to encourage monitoring through closed-circuit television as a method to combat crime and improve public safety.

This bill establishes a framework for the expanded use and regulation of CCTV (closed-circuit television) systems across the UK. It aims to standardise monitoring practices, set requirements for how CCTV footage is stored and accessed, and promote investment in camera technology for public spaces, transport hubs, and potentially private premises. The bill creates oversight mechanisms to balance security benefits with privacy protections, and may include incentives for councils or businesses to install systems. It essentially creates clearer rules for who can use CCTV, how, and for what purposes.

This bill would make it illegal in the UK to develop or acquire cluster munitions. Cluster munitions are weapons that open up in mid-air and scatter many smaller bombs across a large area, making them difficult to control and posing serious risks to civilians. The bill aims to prevent their use and creation in Britain.

This bill would give unmarried couples who live together long-term some of the same legal rights that married couples currently have. Currently, if an unmarried partner dies or the relationship ends, the other person has very limited legal protection, this bill aims to change that.

This bill would ban 'upward-only rent review clauses' in commercial leases (like shops and offices). Currently, some landlords can force tenants to accept rent increases but never decreases. This bill would prevent that, so rent could only stay the same or decrease when reviewed, giving business tenants more protection.

This bill aims to repeal the Inclosure Acts, old laws from the 1700s-1800s that allowed landowners to fence off and privatise common land that communities previously shared. It would restore some of this land to common use, giving local people greater access and control over land in their area.

This bill is designed to give financial help to community amateur sports clubs - the local teams and groups where ordinary people play sports. It mainly does this by giving these clubs tax breaks and other support to make it cheaper for them to operate and help more people get involved in sports.

This bill aims to improve and expand community hospitals - smaller local hospitals that treat patients who don't need to go to large city hospitals. It would help keep basic healthcare services available in local areas across the UK.

This bill creates a Community Wealth Fund - essentially a pot of government money designed to invest in and support local communities across the UK. The aim is to help build stronger local economies by supporting local businesses, creating jobs, and improving community services in areas that need it most.

This bill would make emergency first aid education a required part of the curriculum in all state-funded secondary schools in the UK. Every student would have to learn practical life-saving skills like how to help someone who is choking or unconscious.

This bill changes the rules around 'confiscation orders' - court decisions to take away money, property, or possessions from people convicted of crimes. It aims to make these orders faster and easier to use, particularly in serious criminal cases, so criminals cannot keep or hide the proceeds of their illegal activities.

This Act allows the government to release money from the Consolidated Fund (the main government money account) to pay for essential public services and government operations when needed. It's essentially giving permission for day-to-day government spending to happen between major budget decisions.

This Act gives the UK government official permission to spend taxpayers' money on running the country for the 2009-2010 financial year. It's basically the government's yearly 'shopping list' that Parliament approves, allowing them to pay for services like hospitals, schools, and the military.

This bill would require the UK government to set up a constitutional convention - essentially a national discussion about how Britain's government and laws should work. Currently, much of the UK constitution is unwritten and based on tradition; this bill aims to bring people together to debate whether our system needs updating for modern times.

This bill deals with 'parliamentary privileges' - the special rights and protections that MPs and House of Lords members have so they can do their job without fear. The bill aims to clarify what these privileges are and how they should be used, though the specific details would become clearer as the bill progresses through Parliament.

This bill proposes changes to the UK's constitutional arrangements - essentially the basic rules and structures of how government operates. The bill is currently at an early stage (2nd reading) where MPs debate whether it's worth examining further, though the specific details of what reforms are included aren't provided in this information.

This bill proposes changes to the UK's constitutional arrangements - essentially how our government is organized and run. The specific reforms aren't detailed here, but the bill is in early stages where MPs will debate what changes should be made to the constitution and whether they're necessary.

This bill aims to review and update the UK's constitution (the rules and principles that govern how government works). The UK's constitution isn't written in one document like some countries have, so this bill would examine whether it needs modernizing to suit 21st-century Britain.

This bill changes how construction companies handle 'retention money' - money that clients hold back from payments as security until work is finished. Instead of companies keeping this money themselves, the bill requires it to be held in protected deposit accounts, making sure workers and smaller suppliers actually get paid if something goes wrong.

This bill aims to stop companies from charging customers twice for a single purchase or service. It would make it illegal to double-charge consumers and give people clearer rights to claim refunds and compensation if a company takes their money more than once by mistake or on purpose.

This bill sets up a support scheme to help people who were harmed by contaminated blood products (mainly during the 1970s-1990s) and their families. It establishes how the government will provide compensation and financial help to infected individuals and those who lost loved ones due to this public health disaster.

This bill creates a support scheme for people infected with HIV or hepatitis C through contaminated blood transfusions or blood products (a major health scandal in the 1970s-80s), and for families of those who died. It aims to provide financial compensation and access to healthcare support to help affected people and acknowledge the serious harm caused.

This Act allows the government to use the 'Contingencies Fund' - a pot of emergency money - to pay for urgent, unexpected expenses without getting Parliament's approval first. The government must later tell Parliament what the money was spent on, but it can access the funds immediately when needed for genuine emergencies.

This bill aims to boost renewable energy in the UK by making it simpler to build wind farms on land. It does this by introducing 'contracts for difference' - agreements that guarantee renewable energy companies a set price for their electricity, reducing their financial risk and encouraging investment in clean energy.

This bill aims to make conversion therapy illegal across the UK. Conversion therapy refers to attempts to change someone's sexual orientation or gender identity through treatments or practices - something medical experts say is harmful and ineffective. The bill would prevent people from offering or promoting these practices.

This Act sets out the legal framework for how co-operatives and community benefit societies (businesses owned and run by their members for shared benefit) must be registered, managed, and operated in the UK. It ensures these organisations follow proper rules to protect members' money and interests.

This bill aims to make it easier for co-operative and community benefit societies to invest in environmentally sustainable projects. These are organisations owned and run by their members (like credit unions or housing co-ops), and the bill would help them invest in things like renewable energy and green initiatives while still operating successfully.

This bill updates and improves the legal framework for three types of organisations: co-operatives (businesses owned by workers or members), community benefit societies (organisations that benefit local communities), and credit unions (financial groups that lend money to members). The changes aim to make it easier for these groups to operate and grow while protecting members' interests.

This Act sets out the legal rules for how co-operatives, community benefit societies, and credit unions should be run in the UK. It covers things like how they're registered, how they manage members' money, and what they must do to stay registered and trustworthy.

This bill aims to help co-operatives (businesses owned and run by their members) and social enterprises (businesses that exist mainly to help society, not just make profit) grow stronger. It would provide them with better access to funding, training, and support to create more jobs and community benefits across the UK.

This bill creates a new legal framework for co-operative housing, where groups of people can own and manage homes together rather than through traditional individual ownership or landlords. Members would share decision-making and costs, similar to how food co-ops or credit unions work, but applied to housing.

The Co-operative Housing Tenure Bill establishes a new legal framework for co-operative housing in the UK, where residents collectively own and manage their homes rather than renting from a landlord or purchasing individually. The bill creates formal recognition of housing co-operatives as a distinct tenure type, sets out governance standards, and provides legal protections for co-operative members. It aims to make co-operative housing more accessible and sustainable by clarifying property rights, financing mechanisms, and member responsibilities within a regulated structure.

This bill would allow schools in the UK to operate as co-operatives, meaning they're run jointly by staff, parents, and the community working together as equal partners. Instead of one person or organization controlling the school, everyone involved would have a share in decisions about how it's managed.

This bill aims to encourage more UK workers to own a share of the companies they work for, similar to co-operative or mutual business models. The government would likely offer financial incentives to make it easier for employees to buy into their workplace, giving them a say in how the business is run.

This bill allows co-operatives (businesses owned and run by their members together) to sell a new type of investment called 'permanent shares'. These are long-term investments where shareholders get a share of profits but less control than regular members, helping co-operatives raise money more easily.

This Act updates the laws governing co-operatives (member-owned businesses), mutuals (member-owned financial organizations), and friendly societies (member-run insurance clubs). It aims to make it easier for these types of organizations to operate while keeping rules in place to protect the people who own and use them.

The Coronavirus Act 2020 was emergency legislation that gave the government and public services special powers to handle the COVID-19 crisis. It allowed rules to be changed quickly, provided financial help to workers and businesses, and made it easier for the NHS to operate during the pandemic.

This bill aims to change how coroners (officials who investigate unexplained deaths) decide whether a death was suicide. Currently, coroners must be 'sure beyond reasonable doubt' - the same standard used in criminal courts. The bill would clarify what evidence coroners should consider when making these difficult decisions.

This bill aims to set and enforce better safety and quality standards for cosmetic surgery procedures (like breast implants, facelifts, and liposuction) across the UK. It would ensure clinics, surgeons, and facilities meet certain requirements to protect patients from harm and poor-quality treatment.

This bill deals with council tax valuation bands - the system used to put homes into different groups (A through H) based on their value, which determines how much council tax you pay. The bill would make changes to how this valuation system works, though the specific details aren't yet clear at this early stage.

This bill proposes to reform the council tax valuation bands system. Council tax is the local tax that households pay, and it's currently based on property values from 1991. The bill would likely update how homes are sorted into different value bands to reflect modern-day property prices.

The Counter-Terrorism Act 2008 gives UK police and security services enhanced powers to investigate, monitor, and prevent terrorist activities. It includes measures like extended detention periods for suspects, better information-sharing between agencies, and tools to disrupt terrorist funding and planning.

This Act strengthens UK laws against terrorism and border control. It gives police and security services more powers to investigate suspected terrorists, control who enters the country, and punish those involved in terrorism-related activities. It also creates new offences related to travelling abroad for terrorism purposes.

This bill makes changes to the existing counter-terrorism laws from 2015. It adjusts how the government can monitor potential threats and deals with other security measures, though the specific amendments aren't detailed in the information provided.

This Act toughens the UK's response to terrorism by increasing prison sentences for terror-related crimes, allowing courts to extend sentences for dangerous offenders, and giving authorities stronger powers to monitor and prevent terrorist activities. It aims to make it harder for terrorists to operate and to punish them more severely when caught.

The Courts (Remote Hearings) Bill enables courts across England and Wales to conduct legal proceedings via video link and other remote technologies, rather than requiring all parties to be physically present in a courtroom. The bill provides a legal framework that allows judges to decide when remote hearings are appropriate, covering civil cases, criminal proceedings, and tribunal hearings. It aims to improve access to justice, reduce delays caused by geographical barriers or scheduling conflicts, and cut costs for court users. The bill maintains safeguards to ensure fair trials and allows judges to require in-person hearings when they believe it's necessary for justice.

This bill aims to identify and help people and businesses who didn't qualify for any of the government's Covid-19 financial support schemes during the pandemic. It would provide additional financial assistance to those who were left without help despite being affected by lockdowns and business closures.

This bill proposes to establish a system to compensate UK citizens who claim they have experienced serious health problems as a direct result of receiving a Covid-19 vaccine. It would create a process for people to apply for financial support if they can demonstrate vaccine-related harm.

This bill proposes a system for people in the UK who believe they have suffered serious health damage from a Covid-19 vaccine to claim financial compensation. It would set out how people could apply for payments and what injuries would qualify for support, similar to compensation schemes that exist for other medical treatments.

This bill proposes to create or change a system for handling claims from people who say they've been harmed by Covid-19 vaccines. It would set up a process for these claims to be assessed and potentially for people to receive compensation, similar to schemes that exist for damage caused by other medicines.

This bill would establish a compensation scheme for people who have suffered serious adverse health effects they believe were caused by Covid-19 vaccines. It would create a legal framework allowing individuals to claim damages without having to prove negligence by vaccine manufacturers or the government. The scheme would cover medical costs, loss of earnings, and other damages for those who can demonstrate a causal link between vaccination and their injury. This differs from the existing Vaccine Damage Payment scheme, which has strict eligibility criteria and provides only £120,000 maximum compensation.

This bill would create a new government compensation scheme for people who have suffered serious, lasting health damage that they believe was caused by receiving a Covid-19 vaccine. Similar schemes already exist for other vaccines, and this would work in a comparable way, with the government providing financial payments to approved claimants.

This bill would set up a system to pay money to people in the UK who suffered serious health damage that they can prove was caused by a Covid-19 vaccine. It's similar to existing schemes for other vaccines, and would help affected people with costs like medical treatment and income they lost while unwell.

This bill would establish a system to pay compensation to people in the UK who believe they have suffered serious health damage as a direct result of receiving a Covid-19 vaccine. It's similar to existing schemes that compensate people harmed by other medicines or vaccines.

This bill establishes a compensation scheme for people who have suffered severe adverse health effects from Covid-19 vaccines administered in the UK. It creates a legal framework and funding mechanism to provide payments to vaccine-injured individuals without requiring them to prove negligence or fault on the part of vaccine manufacturers or the NHS. The scheme would operate similarly to existing vaccine damage payment schemes, offering financial support to those who meet specific medical criteria for serious injury. The bill aims to provide a faster, more accessible route to compensation than pursuing traditional legal claims.

This bill gives the government legal authority to diagnose Covid-19 infections and provide vaccine treatments to UK citizens. It's currently being debated in Parliament to decide whether these powers should be formally approved in law.

This bill gives the government legal authority to diagnose Covid-19 and provide vaccine treatments to the public. It's currently being debated in parliament to decide whether these powers should be formally approved, extended, or changed in some way.

This bill aims to add new financial regulations to combat child sexual abuse material by requiring banks, payment systems, and credit providers to better monitor and prevent their services being used for CSAM-related crimes. It focuses on cutting off the money flow that supports this illegal activity.

The Crime and Policing Bill is a legislative package designed to strengthen law enforcement powers and modernise the police service across England and Wales. It typically includes measures to expand police stop-and-search authorities, introduce new criminal offences (particularly around protest activities), enhance sentencing powers, and reform police conduct procedures. The bill aims to give officers additional tools to combat crime and anti-social behaviour while addressing public concerns about safety and disorder.

This bill would allow members of the public to petition Parliament to trigger a review of criminal cases through the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC). Currently, only the CCRC itself can decide which cases to investigate for potential miscarriages of justice. The bill creates a formal mechanism for citizens to submit evidence of potential wrongful convictions and require the CCRC to consider these petitions seriously. This could increase public scrutiny of the criminal justice system and potentially lead to more cases being re-examined for procedural errors or new evidence.

This bill requires a formal review of the Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority (CICA), the public body that awards compensation to victims of violent crime in England, Scotland, and Wales. The review would examine how the CICA operates, including its decision-making processes, eligibility criteria, award levels, and efficiency. The bill aims to assess whether the current system adequately serves crime victims and whether changes are needed to improve how compensation claims are handled and processed.

This bill asks Parliament to take a close look at the Criminal Injuries Compensation Scheme - the system that gives money to people who have been victims of violent crime. A review would check if the scheme is still fair and fit for purpose in 2024.

This bill changes the rules about criminal records in the UK. It likely focuses on things like: which convictions should be disclosed, how long records are kept, and whether people with old convictions can have them hidden from employers or the public. The exact details matter a lot - this is why Parliament is debating it.

The Crossrail Act 2008 is a law that allows the government to build a new high-speed railway line running east to west across London and into surrounding areas. It gives the project legal permission and powers to acquire land, manage construction, and operate the new railway service (now known as the Elizabeth Line).

This bill would change the rules about who can work for the Crown (government and public sector organisations). Currently, most Crown jobs must go to British citizens, but this bill would allow non-British citizens to apply and work in these positions.

This bill would change the rules so that non-British citizens can apply for and work in jobs for the Crown (the UK government and its organizations). Currently, most of these jobs require you to be a British citizen, but this bill would relax that requirement to open up employment opportunities to people from other countries.

This bill requires organisations that fall victim to ransomware attacks or cyber extortion to report the incident to the relevant authorities within a specified timeframe. It aims to create a comprehensive database of cyber threats targeting UK businesses and institutions, helping law enforcement and cybersecurity agencies identify patterns, track criminals, and coordinate responses. The bill likely includes penalties for non-compliance and may establish exemptions for cases where reporting poses genuine security risks. By mandating disclosure, the government seeks to improve situational awareness of cyber threats and strengthen the UK's collective defence against organised cybercriminals.

This bill updates UK cyber security law by replacing the outdated Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018 with new, stricter requirements for organisations that provide essential services and digital infrastructure. It requires critical sectors, such as energy, water, healthcare, and financial services, to implement stronger security measures, report cyber incidents faster, and comply with regular security audits. The bill also expands protections to cover more businesses in the digital sector and gives regulators stronger enforcement powers to penalise non-compliance, aiming to reduce vulnerability to cyber attacks that could harm public safety and national security.

This bill aims to improve how people suffering from asbestos-related illnesses can claim financial compensation. Asbestos is a dangerous material that was widely used in buildings and products; this bill would make it fairer and simpler for victims to get money from those responsible for their exposure, particularly in cases where the original source is unclear or the responsible company no longer exists.

This bill proposes amendments to the Dangerous Dogs Act 1991, which currently restricts ownership of certain dog breeds deemed high-risk (including pit bull type dogs). The amendments would modify how dangerous dogs are identified, regulated, and managed. The specific changes would depend on the amendment's provisions, potentially altering breed-specific legislation, changing assessment procedures, or adjusting penalties for owners. The bill aims to update 30+ year old legislation to reflect current dog behaviour science and public safety standards.

The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 reforms how organisations in the UK can collect, use, and share data. It establishes new rules giving individuals greater control over their personal information, requiring companies to be more transparent about data use, and creating pathways for researchers and public bodies to access data more easily for legitimate purposes like health research and policy-making. The bill aims to balance privacy protection with enabling beneficial uses of data by establishing clearer legal frameworks and enforcement mechanisms.

This bill proposes changing how the UK manages daylight saving time, the practice of moving clocks forward an hour in spring and back an hour in autumn. Rather than continuing this twice-yearly switch, the bill would likely introduce permanent clock times, meaning we'd either stay on one time year-round or change how the system operates. The exact changes depend on which version of the bill passes through Parliament.

The Debt Relief (Developing Countries) Bill enables the UK government to write off or reduce debts owed by developing countries, typically through bilateral agreements or multilateral initiatives. The bill provides the legal framework for the government to forgive loans that developing nations cannot feasibly repay, with the aim of freeing up resources in those countries for essential services like healthcare and education. This would apply to debts owed directly to the UK government rather than private creditors, and would likely be coordinated with other creditor nations to ensure fair burden-sharing.

This bill would transfer power over employment and workplace rules from the UK Parliament in Westminster to the Scottish Parliament in Edinburgh. It would allow Scotland to set its own employment laws rather than following UK-wide rules, giving Scottish politicians more say over how work is regulated in Scotland.

This bill aims to transfer more government power from Parliament in London to local councils and regional authorities across England. It would let different areas make more decisions about their own services and policies rather than following one-size-fits-all rules set by central government.

This Act allowed the UK government to give broadcasters and companies information about where people lived during the digital TV switchover (around 2008-2012). The information helped these companies contact people who needed help moving from old analogue TV signals to new digital ones, but it meant sharing personal data on a large scale.

This bill aims to require that digitally altered images, particularly those that change body shape, size, or appearance, are clearly labeled or marked so viewers know they've been edited. The goal is to tackle the negative effects of unrealistic filtered images on people's self-image and mental wellbeing, especially among young people.

This bill aims to tackle the problem of heavily filtered and edited body images on social media and in adverts. It would require that digitally altered images - like those with smoothed skin, reshaped bodies, or extreme filters - must be clearly labelled so viewers know they're not realistic. The goal is to protect people's mental health, especially young people who might feel pressured to look like impossible edited versions of real bodies.

This bill would require the UK's diplomatic service (embassies and government representatives abroad) to prioritize serving UK-produced wines and sparkling wines at official events and functions. It's designed to support British wine producers by giving their products prominence when the country is representing itself internationally.

This bill aims to tackle the employment gap for disabled people in the UK. It would likely introduce measures to help disabled people get jobs and stay in work, addressing the fact that disabled people are less likely to be employed than non-disabled people.

This bill asks the government to review Disabled Facilities Grants - money that helps disabled people pay for home improvements like ramps, grab rails, or accessible bathrooms. The review would check if the system is working properly and if changes are needed to make it better for disabled people and their families.

This bill aims to make it a crime to leave needles abandoned in public spaces like streets, parks, or beaches. It would introduce legal penalties for people who discard needles irresponsibly, with the goal of reducing the risk of needle-stick injuries that can spread serious diseases like HIV and hepatitis.

This bill aims to control or ban the sale and use of single-use disposable barbecues (the small charcoal ones sold in shops). It's designed to reduce the risk of wildfires and accidental fires in outdoor spaces where these barbecues are often left unattended or not properly extinguished.

This bill aims to address the problems caused by disposable barbecues, such as wildfires, injuries, and litter in outdoor spaces, by restricting their sale or use. It's a response to incidents where cheap, single-use barbecues have caused damage to landscapes and put people at risk.

This bill would make it illegal to sell disposable e-cigarettes in the UK. Currently, people can buy single-use vapes that are thrown away after the battery runs out. The bill aims to stop this by prohibiting their sale, similar to how some other countries have already done.

This Act changed the rules about when UK general elections happen. Instead of elections being automatically held every five years on a fixed date, it gives the Prime Minister more freedom to decide when to call an election (within certain limits). Essentially, it replaced the Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011, which had locked election dates in place.

This bill changes the financial rules for divorce in England and Wales. When married couples split up, they have to divide their money, pensions, and property - this bill would alter how those decisions are made by the courts.

This bill aims to encourage and support British doctors and nurses to work in developing countries. It likely removes barriers that prevent medical staff from taking time to help in poorer nations, either through voluntary work, short-term placements, or aid programmes.

This bill strengthens consumer protections for people commissioning domestic building works (such as extensions, renovations, and repairs to homes). It establishes clearer standards for builder conduct, requires better transparency in contracts and pricing, and creates enforcement mechanisms to hold builders accountable for poor workmanship or non-completion. The bill aims to reduce disputes between homeowners and builders by setting baseline requirements for qualifications, insurance, and dispute resolution before work begins.

This bill proposes to lower the Value Added Tax (VAT) on domestic energy - the tax people pay when they buy gas and electricity for their homes. Currently VAT is charged at the standard rate; this bill would reduce it, meaning households would see lower energy bills.

This bill proposes to reduce the Value Added Tax (VAT) rate on domestic energy bills, electricity, gas, and heating oil for household use, from the current 5% to 0%. The measure aims to lower household energy costs by removing the VAT charged on these essential utilities. The bill would apply to residential customers and is intended to help reduce energy bills during a period of high energy prices and to ease the cost-of-living burden on UK households.

This bill requires the government to launch a formal call for evidence on how to improve energy efficiency in UK homes. Rather than implementing specific new policies immediately, it first gathers information from experts, businesses, homeowners, and other stakeholders about what measures work best and are most cost-effective. The bill aims to inform future policy decisions on reducing household energy consumption and carbon emissions through better insulation, heating systems, and building standards. It essentially pauses for data collection before major legislative changes are made to domestic energy efficiency requirements.

This bill aims to improve how much energy UK homes waste by making them more efficient. It would likely involve government support (possibly funding or grants) to help people upgrade their homes with better heating, insulation, and other energy-saving improvements.

This bill sets rules to make homes more energy-efficient by reducing wasted heat and power. It likely requires homes to meet certain energy performance standards, similar to how cars have fuel efficiency ratings, to help people save money and protect the environment.

This bill aims to introduce stronger penalties specifically for people caught drink driving for a second or subsequent time. It's designed to punish repeat offenders more severely than first-time offenders, with the goal of stopping people from drink driving again and making roads safer.

This bill aims to automatically suspend driving instructors from their job if they are convicted of sexual offences. It's designed to protect learner drivers, particularly young and vulnerable people, by keeping convicted offenders out of one-on-one teaching situations where they have power over their students.

This bill makes changes to the laws about driving offences (breaking driving rules). However, the specific details of what is being changed aren't clear from the information provided - Parliament would need to see the full bill text to understand exactly what driving offences are being added, removed, or changed.

This bill allows police officers to conduct roadside drug tests on drivers they suspect of being under the influence of drugs. It aims to catch drug-impaired drivers quickly and reduce drug-driving accidents, similar to how current breath tests work for alcohol.

This bill aims to change education law so that students' non-religious philosophical beliefs (such as humanism, atheism, or secular worldviews) receive the same legal recognition and protection that religious beliefs currently have in schools. Currently, the law mainly focuses on protecting religious convictions, so this bill would extend those same safeguards to non-religious students.

This bill aims to improve how schools and councils support students with special educational needs - those who have disabilities, learning difficulties, or other challenges affecting their education. It likely changes rules about how these students are assessed, what help they receive, and how schools fund and deliver this support.

This bill would require schools in England to actively teach and promote 'British values' as a core part of the curriculum. It seeks to embed values such as democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, and mutual respect across all educational settings.
