The bill aims to ensure that students develop a stronger understanding of British civic culture and constitutional principles. Schools would need to demonstrate how these values are integrated into teaching, potentially through dedicated lessons, assemblies, or cross-curricular approaches.

This bill would require people to prove who they are by showing identification before they can vote in UK elections. Currently, voters don't need to show ID - they just give their name and address. The bill would change this rule, though the exact type of ID accepted hasn't been fully detailed yet since it's still at an early stage.

This Act changed how people register to vote in the UK. It moved away from a household-based system to individual voter registration, meaning each person must now register themselves rather than one person registering everyone at an address. It also updated various rules about elections and how they are run.

This bill would change UK law to allow electric personal vehicles (such as e-scooters and electric skateboards) to be legally used on public roads and highways. Currently, most of these vehicles aren't allowed on roads, and this bill aims to create rules so they can be used safely alongside cars and pedestrians.

This bill would make it legal for people to use electric personal vehicles (such as e-scooters and electric skateboards) on highways and public roads in the UK. Currently, many of these vehicles exist in a legal grey area, so this bill would set clear rules about how and where they can be used.

This bill establishes legal standards and regulations for electrically assisted pedal cycles (e-bikes) in the UK. It defines what qualifies as an e-bike, sets safety and performance requirements, and clarifies where and how they can be used on public roads and paths. The bill aims to create consistency across the country while balancing the growth of e-bike usage with road safety and environmental goals.

This bill requires the government to carry out a formal review of the UK's electricity grid - the network of cables and equipment that brings power to our homes and businesses. The review will check if the grid is fit for the future and working as efficiently as possible.

This bill aims to control how e-cigarettes are advertised and who can buy them in the UK. It would set a legal age limit for purchasing e-cigarettes (like we have for cigarettes) and restrict how companies can advertise these products, particularly to prevent them reaching young people.

This bill would introduce new laws to control how e-cigarettes are branded, promoted and advertised in the UK. It aims to restrict things like adverts, sponsorships and eye-catching packaging, with the main goal of preventing young people from being attracted to e-cigarettes and potentially getting addicted to nicotine.

This bill aims to bring in new rules for e-cigarettes and vaping products in the UK. It would control things like where they can be sold, how they're advertised, age restrictions for buyers, and possibly the ingredients allowed in them. The goal is to protect young people from vaping while balancing the needs of adults.

This bill introduces new regulations for electronic cigarettes and vaping products in the UK. It gives the government powers to control how e-cigarettes are made, packaged, advertised, and sold to protect public health, especially to prevent young people from using them.

This bill aims to make it easier for doctors and hospitals across the NHS to access and share electronic patient records with each other. The goal is to improve continuity of care by ensuring that all healthcare professionals treating you have access to the same up-to-date medical information, rather than having records scattered across different systems.

This bill would require schools in England to teach emergency and life-saving skills as part of the curriculum. Students would learn practical techniques including cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), the recovery position, how to use automated external defibrillators (AEDs), and how to respond to choking, bleeding, and other medical emergencies. The bill aims to equip young people with knowledge that could help them save lives in emergency situations before professional medical help arrives.

This bill aims to give workers on zero-hours contracts (where employers don't guarantee any minimum hours) the right to a guaranteed minimum number of working hours each week. This would make their pay and schedules more predictable and stable.

This bill would legally require employers to make reasonable changes to help people who are carers keep their jobs. For example, a worker caring for an elderly parent could ask for different hours or work-from-home options, and their employer would have to seriously consider this request rather than refuse it.

This bill aims to protect workers from being unfairly dismissed and then re-hired on worse terms. It targets a practice where employers fire workers (especially union members) and offer them their job back with lower pay or worse conditions, forcing workers to accept or lose their job. The bill would make this tactic illegal or more difficult.

This bill aims to protect workers from being dismissed and then rehired on worse conditions, particularly those involved in trade union activities. It stops employers from using dismissal and re-engagement as a way to reduce pay, change contracts, or weaken workers' rights.

This bill gives the Welsh Government greater control over employment support services in Wales, rather than these services being run by the UK Government. It allows Wales to design and deliver its own job-support schemes to help unemployed and disadvantaged people find work.

This bill aims to stop employers from treating people unfairly at work because of their insurance status or medical history. It would make it illegal to refuse someone a job, deny them promotion, or treat them badly based on insurance-related factors, similar to existing protections against discrimination.

This bill proposes changes to employment law in the UK - the rules that govern how employers and employees should treat each other at work. The exact details of what it changes aren't fully specified here, but it's currently being debated in Parliament to decide if it should become law.

This bill aims to expand parental leave rights so both mothers and fathers can share time off after having a baby, and to strengthen workers' rights to request flexible working arrangements (like part-time hours or working from home). The goal is to help parents balance work and family life more easily.

This bill aims to give clearer legal definitions of different types of employment status in the UK. Currently, the rules about who counts as an employee versus self-employed can be confusing, so this bill tries to make it simpler and fairer for both workers and businesses.

The Employment Status (Review) Bill creates a mechanism to review and clarify the employment status of workers in the UK, particularly those in ambiguous positions like gig economy workers, freelancers, and contractors. The bill aims to establish clearer definitions and tests to determine whether individuals should be classified as employees, workers, or self-employed, which affects their rights to minimum wage, holiday pay, and pension contributions. It may introduce a statutory definition or review process to resolve disputes about employment classification that currently create uncertainty for both workers and employers. The legislation responds to growing concerns that many workers lack basic protections because their status remains legally unclear.

The Energy Act 2016 reformed the UK's energy market to accelerate the transition to low-carbon electricity and reduce emissions. It introduced the Contracts for Difference scheme, which guarantees stable prices for renewable energy generators, making investment in wind, solar, and nuclear power more attractive. The Act also reformed electricity market rules, enhanced consumer protections, and established the Oil and Gas Authority to regulate North Sea energy production more efficiently.

This bill aims to protect vulnerable energy consumers by introducing two main measures: regulating pre-payment meter charges to prevent users from paying significantly more than standard customers, and requiring energy suppliers to offer affordable 'social tariffs' to low-income households. Pre-payment meters currently often charge higher unit rates despite being used disproportionately by poorer households, and this bill seeks to cap that premium. The social tariff requirement would create a dedicated low-cost energy option for struggling families, similar to schemes already operating in some European countries.

This bill sets energy efficiency standards for Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) - these are homes rented out to several unrelated people, like student houses or shared flats. It would require landlords to make improvements such as better insulation and efficient heating to reduce energy waste and costs for tenants.

This bill aims to help reduce energy waste in buildings and make energy bills cheaper for people across the UK. It would likely set new standards for how efficiently homes and businesses use energy, and potentially introduce programmes or requirements to improve insulation, heating systems and other energy-saving measures.

This bill aims to tackle two problems at once: reducing carbon emissions from energy production to fight climate change, and making sure more people can afford to heat their homes properly. It would put new requirements on energy companies and direct money towards making homes warmer and more energy-efficient.

This bill aims to help the UK use energy more efficiently and cost-effectively. It would introduce measures to reduce energy waste and help people and businesses lower their energy bills, likely through improved standards for buildings, appliances, or energy practices.

This bill aims to protect off-grid households from high energy prices. Many rural homes can't access mains gas, so they rely on expensive alternatives like heating oil and LPG. The bill would introduce measures to make these energy sources more affordable and fair in price, similar to how on-grid households benefit from regulated gas prices.

This bill proposes changing how the UK uses daylight saving time (clock changes) to save energy. Currently we change clocks twice a year - the bill would either stop these changes or make daylight saving permanent, aiming to use natural daylight better and reduce energy costs.

The English Devolution and Community Empowerment Bill transfers powers from central government to local areas and communities across England. It enables regions to have greater control over decisions affecting them, such as economic development, transport, and public services, through devolved authorities. The bill also strengthens community involvement in local decision-making by giving residents and organisations more say in how public money is spent and services are delivered. This represents a shift toward 'levelling up' by allowing different areas to develop policies suited to their specific needs rather than following one-size-fits-all Westminster approaches.

The Environment Bill sets new laws to protect the UK's air, water, and wildlife. It creates responsibilities for the government and businesses to meet environmental targets, tackle pollution, and restore natural habitats. It also aims to reduce single-use plastics and improve recycling.

This bill aims to improve how fly-tipping (illegally dumping rubbish on land) is reported and dealt with. It would likely create better systems for people to report fly-tipping and help councils and environmental agencies track and stop it more effectively.

This bill would change the rules around titles (like 'Lord', 'Lady', 'Sir', 'Dame') so that people can use titles that match their gender identity rather than being locked into titles based on their sex at birth. It's designed to make titles more inclusive for transgender and non-binary people.

The E-scooters (Review and Awareness) Bill requires the government to conduct a comprehensive review of e-scooter use and safety across the UK, and to launch a public awareness campaign about the risks and regulations. The bill focuses on gathering data about e-scooter accidents, injuries, and usage patterns, while also improving public understanding of where e-scooters can legally be used. It does not directly introduce new laws or bans, but instead mandates investigation and education to inform future policy decisions.

This bill aims to ban 'essay mills' - companies that write essays and assignments for students in exchange for money. It would make it illegal to provide or use these services, helping to stop cheating in universities and colleges across the UK.

This Act requires the UK Parliament to hold referendums (public votes) before the government can agree to major new powers for the European Union or significant changes to UK-EU relations. It's designed to make sure big EU decisions are approved by British voters, not just politicians.

This Act allows the UK Parliament to approve Croatia's membership in the European Union and gives Ireland an opt-out from certain EU justice and law enforcement rules. It's mainly a formal legal step to update UK law to match these EU changes.

This bill is designed to make sure Parliament carefully considers all the ways that leaving the EU will affect the UK - including changes to laws, trade agreements, and people's rights. It aims to ensure the government plans properly for these big changes rather than rushing decisions.

This bill aims to make sure the UK government gives Parliament and citizens more information about European Union matters. It would require the government to be more transparent and open about EU-related decisions, negotiations, and their impacts on the UK.

This bill sets out new rules for how the UK government must collect, store, and share information about European Union matters. It aims to make sure Parliament and the public can access EU-related documents and information more easily after Brexit.

This bill requires the UK government to provide more public information and reports about European Union issues and activities. It aims to increase openness and allow Parliament and citizens to better understand what the government is doing regarding EU-related matters.

This bill provides the legal framework for the UK to leave the European Union under the withdrawal agreement negotiated between the UK government and the EU. It implements the agreement that was finalized in October 2019, which includes a transition period (now ended) during which UK-EU relations would be governed by existing EU law. The bill ratifies the withdrawal agreement in UK law, establishes the legal mechanisms for the transition, and creates provisions for the UK-EU relationship after this period ends. Essentially, it makes the negotiated Brexit deal enforceable under British law.

This Act gave Parliament the legal power to block a no-deal Brexit and required the government to ask for more time from the EU if no agreement had been reached by October 31st, 2019. Essentially, it stopped the Prime Minister from forcing the UK out of the EU without a deal that Parliament had approved.

This bill sets up a transition (or 'implementation') period after Brexit where the UK temporarily keeps following EU rules and laws while both sides negotiate what their relationship will be like in the future. Think of it as a bridge period rather than an immediate cliff-edge change, giving businesses and government time to prepare for the new arrangements.

This bill aims to allow government officials and public bodies more freedom to make sensible decisions based on individual situations, rather than mechanically following strict rules in every case. It would give decision-makers permission to use reasonable judgment when they think it's fair and appropriate to do so.

This bill would make it illegal for people to wear face coverings that hide their identity in public spaces across the UK. It would prevent people from wearing items like full-face masks, veils, or hoods in most situations, with potential exceptions for safety equipment or medical reasons.

This bill aims to help people in debt by requiring fee-charging debt management companies to promote free debt advice services instead. The goal is to make sure people know they can get help with their debts without having to pay money to a company.

This bill would create a legal right for employees undergoing fertility treatment to take paid time off work for medical appointments and procedures. It would require employers to grant reasonable time off for activities such as clinic visits, egg collection, embryo transfer, and related treatments, without loss of pay or penalties to employment status. The bill aims to reduce the financial and practical barriers that prevent people from accessing fertility treatment, which can be time-intensive and emotionally demanding. It would apply across the UK to employees in both public and private sectors.

The Financial Assistance to Ukraine Act 2025 authorizes the UK government to provide financial aid to Ukraine, likely including grants, loans, or both to support Ukraine's government operations, military defence, and post-conflict reconstruction. The bill establishes a legal framework allowing Treasury spending on Ukrainian assistance without requiring individual parliamentary votes for each disbursement. This enables the UK to respond quickly to Ukraine's evolving needs during its conflict with Russia and contribute to Ukraine's long-term stability and recovery.

The Financial Education Bill aims to improve financial literacy among UK citizens by mandating financial education in schools and establishing frameworks for public financial awareness programmes. The bill requires schools to teach practical money management skills, including budgeting, savings, debt management, and investment basics, as part of the curriculum. It also establishes funding mechanisms for financial education initiatives targeted at underserved communities and vulnerable groups. The legislation seeks to reduce financial exclusion and improve long-term economic wellbeing by ensuring citizens have foundational knowledge about managing personal finances.

This bill gives financial regulators stronger powers to supervise and control how derivatives (bets on future prices of things like oil, currencies, or shares) are bought and sold in the UK. It aims to make the financial system safer by preventing excessive risk-taking with these complex products.

This bill aims to make sure people living in or visiting buildings have clear, easy-to-access information about how to escape safely in a fire. It would require buildings to better communicate fire safety rules and procedures so everyone knows what to do in an emergency.

This bill strengthens protections by requiring firearms and shotgun licensing authorities to consider domestic violence history when deciding whether to grant or renew licenses. It mandates that anyone with a conviction or restraining order related to domestic violence faces automatic scrutiny in the licensing process, and authorities must actively share relevant information between agencies. The bill aims to prevent individuals with a pattern of domestic abuse from accessing firearms, recognizing that domestic violence is a significant risk factor for firearm-related harm.

This bill aims to tighten the rules around firearm ownership and increase penalties for crimes where someone is attacked because of their race, religion, sexuality, or other characteristics. It combines two policy areas to try to reduce both gun-related harm and hate-based violence in the UK.

This bill aims to tighten the rules around who can own firearms (guns) and to increase penalties for crimes where the victim is targeted because of their identity, such as their race, religion, disability, or sexual orientation. It combines two separate issues: making firearm ownership stricter and making hate-motivated crimes punished more severely.

This bill makes changes to the Fireworks Act 2003, which is the law controlling fireworks in the UK. The exact changes aren't detailed here, but the bill would update or modify some of the existing rules about fireworks - for example, this could involve stricter safety checks, age limits, or when fireworks can be used.

This bill aims to regulate Fixed Odds Betting Terminals - the fast-spinning electronic gambling machines in betting shops. It seeks to make them safer by limiting how much money people can bet at once and introducing other measures to protect people from addiction and financial harm caused by problem gambling.

This bill removes the law that set elections to happen every 5 years on a fixed date. If it passes, Prime Ministers will go back to being able to call elections whenever they want (within a 5-year limit), as they could do before 2011.

This bill removes the rule that requires general elections to happen every 5 years on a fixed date. It would let the Prime Minister call elections whenever they want (within a 5-year limit). This reverses a previous law called the Fixed-term Parliaments Act from 2011.

This bill removes a 2011 law that made UK general elections happen automatically every 5 years. If passed, Prime Ministers would go back to having the power to decide when to call an election (within a maximum 5-year limit), rather than elections happening on a fixed date.

This bill aims to make it easier for UK workers to request flexible working arrangements such as remote work, part-time hours, or different schedules. It would require employers to take these requests seriously and only refuse them for genuine business reasons, giving employees more say in how they work.

This bill aims to give UK workers the right to request flexible working arrangements (such as working from home, part-time hours, or different times) more easily. Currently, workers can request this but employers can refuse. The bill would strengthen these rights and potentially require employers to have good reasons if they say no.

This bill proposes setting up a parliamentary committee to investigate foetal sentience - whether an unborn baby can feel pain or sensations, and at what stage of pregnancy this might happen. The committee would gather scientific evidence to help inform future policy decisions about abortion and pregnancy care.

This bill aims to address food insecurity in the UK - meaning situations where people struggle to afford enough healthy food. It would likely create new policies or support systems to help vulnerable people access food and reduce hunger across the country.

This bill aims to improve how food is labelled in shops by requiring clearer, more detailed information on packaging. It could include things like nutrition information, allergen warnings, or country-of-origin labels to help UK shoppers make better-informed decisions about their food.

This bill would require food packaging to display labels showing the environmental impact of what you're buying - such as how much carbon was used to produce it or how much water it needed. It aims to help people understand and choose more sustainable food options.

This bill would require food manufacturers to provide clearer, standardized nutrition information on food packaging and restrict health claims made on food labels. It aims to help UK consumers make more informed dietary choices by making calorie, fat, sugar, and salt content more visible and consistent across all products. The bill also establishes rules about which health claims (such as 'low fat' or 'heart healthy') manufacturers can legally make, requiring them to be backed by scientific evidence. These measures are designed to address obesity, diet-related diseases, and misleading marketing in the food industry.

This bill proposes to update the regulations that control how food packaging must be labelled in the UK. It would change what information food companies must display on their packaging - such as ingredients, allergens, or how healthy the food is - though the exact changes aren't specified in this basic description.

This bill would require the UK government to develop a formal strategy to address food poverty - the problem of people not being able to afford enough nutritious food. It's about creating an official plan to identify the causes of food poverty and set out how the government will tackle it.

This bill establishes new regulatory controls over food products sold in UK markets and strengthens requirements for public sector food procurement (such as in schools, hospitals, and prisons). It likely includes measures to set standards for food quality, labelling, and safety; potentially restricts certain products or ingredients; and requires public institutions to meet specific sourcing or nutritional criteria when purchasing food. The bill aims to protect consumers, support domestic producers, and improve nutritional standards in publicly-funded settings.

This bill aims to introduce new government rules and oversight for English football clubs. It would likely cover areas such as financial rules, spending limits, ownership standards, and how clubs are managed - similar to how other industries are regulated to protect fans, players, and the sport's future.

This bill gives the government new powers to control who attends football matches and other sports events, mainly to reduce crowd violence and anti-social behaviour. It allows for things like banning troublemakers from stadiums and potentially requiring ID cards for entry.

This bill would give the UK government stronger powers to exclude or remove foreign nationals (non-British citizens) from the country if they commit certain crimes. It aims to speed up the process of getting foreign criminal offenders out of the UK.

This bill would require foreign nationals to verify their immigration status in order to use certain public services in the UK. It aims to restrict access to publicly-funded services to British citizens and those with legal immigration rights, though the exact details of which services are affected may be clarified during parliamentary debate.

This bill gives the UK government stronger powers to remove foreign nationals (non-British citizens) from the country if they've committed crimes or are serving prison sentences. The goal is to speed up the process of getting foreign offenders out of the UK, rather than keeping them in British prisons or the country long-term.

This bill sets up official standards and rules for forensic linguists who work with the police and courts. It aims to make sure that when experts analyze language evidence (like text messages or statements), they follow the same reliable methods, so justice isn't based on inconsistent or poor-quality analysis.

This bill creates an official Forensic Science Regulator - a person or role that checks and controls the quality of forensic science used in UK criminal cases. The regulator would set standards for labs and experts to follow, making sure that evidence like DNA tests and fingerprints are accurate before they're used in court.

This Act creates an official Forensic Science Regulator - a person responsible for checking that forensic evidence (like DNA and fingerprints) used in criminal cases is accurate and reliable. They set standards that forensic labs must follow to help make sure justice is done fairly.

This bill aims to automatically register eligible children for free school meals, rather than requiring parents to apply manually. Currently, eligible families must complete application forms to access free meals, which creates a barrier that means some entitled children miss out. The bill would use existing government data to identify eligible children and enroll them automatically, ensuring uptake of the entitlement without parental bureaucracy. This would expand access to free meals for children from low-income households across England.

This bill aims to strengthen legal protections for freedom of expression specifically when discussing religion or belief systems. It would establish clearer boundaries between protected speech (such as criticism of religious ideas, practices, or institutions) and unlawful speech (such as incitement to violence or harassment based on someone's religious identity). The bill seeks to prevent individuals from facing legal consequences or prosecution simply for expressing opinions, analysis, or critique about religious or non-religious beliefs. It essentially clarifies that disagreeing with, questioning, or criticizing religious doctrines is a protected right distinct from attacking or inciting harm against people who hold those beliefs.

The Freight Crime Bill strengthens law enforcement powers to combat theft, robbery, and organised crime targeting goods in transit across the UK. It introduces new offences specifically targeting freight crime, increases maximum prison sentences for related crimes, and gives police enhanced stop-and-search powers and surveillance capabilities. The bill also establishes a national freight crime unit and requires better information-sharing between transport companies, police, and border agencies to disrupt criminal supply chains.

This bill proposes changing child benefit so that parents get more money when their children are young (when childcare and baby costs are highest), rather than spreading the payment equally across all years. It's called 'front-loaded' because the money is loaded towards the front (early years) of a child's life.

This bill would change how child benefit is paid out by giving families more money per child when children are young, then reducing the amount as children get older. Currently, families get the same amount for each child regardless of age, but this bill proposes a 'front-loaded' system that prioritises younger children.

This bill aims to improve access to college and university education for people who currently find it harder to get in, such as students from low-income families or underrepresented groups. It's designed to remove barriers and create more opportunities for a wider range of people to pursue further and higher education.

This bill proposes to change and update the Gambling Act 2005, which is the main law controlling gambling in the UK. The specific amendments aren't detailed here, but the bill aims to modernise gambling rules - possibly to address issues like problem gambling, online betting, or how betting companies operate.

This bill proposes to make Gamma-Butyrolactone (GBL) illegal in the UK. GBL is a chemical that some people use as a recreational drug because of its effects similar to other substances. The bill aims to stop its production, sale, and possession to protect public health and safety.

This bill creates a licensing system to regulate gangmasters - people or companies that hire and supply workers to other businesses. Its main goal is to stop the exploitation of workers by ensuring only legitimate, inspected gangmasters can legally operate, protecting people from poor pay, unsafe work, and bad treatment.

This bill would establish an independent public inquiry into UK involvement in and conduct related to the conflict in Gaza. The inquiry would have statutory powers to compel witnesses, examine documents, and publish findings on matters including UK arms exports, military support, diplomatic actions, and potential breaches of international humanitarian law. The bill aims to create an official, legally-binding investigation with transparent proceedings and a published report, rather than leaving accountability to existing parliamentary or government review mechanisms.

The General Cemetery Act 2025 updates the legal framework governing the operation, maintenance, and regulation of cemeteries across the UK. The bill establishes modern standards for cemetery management, including provisions for digital record-keeping, environmental practices, and consumer protections for families purchasing burial plots. It aims to modernise legislation dating back to the 19th century while addressing contemporary issues such as land use, cremation services, and memorial regulations.

This bill would create rules or requirements for televised debates between political party leaders during general election campaigns. Currently, debates happen but aren't required by law. The bill aims to make sure voters can see leaders debate important issues face-to-face as a standard part of every election.

This bill is designed to provide some kind of public support during general elections. Without more details about the specific proposals, the exact nature of this support isn't yet clear, it could relate to voter information, election funding, or other election-related assistance. The bill is at an early stage and hasn't been fully debated yet.

This bill aims to promote goods and services that are made or produced in the UK. It would likely encourage the government and possibly businesses to prioritize buying British-made products over imports from other countries.

This bill creates new laws to regulate how goods delivery services (like courier and food delivery companies) operate in the UK. It likely covers things such as how delivery workers are treated, delivery standards, safety requirements, or environmental rules - though the exact details aren't clear from the title alone.

This bill creates new legal rules for 'goods mortgages' - a way for people and businesses to borrow money by using their possessions (like machinery, vans, or equipment) as a guarantee that they'll repay the loan. It modernises old laws to make this type of borrowing clearer and more practical for the modern economy.

This bill proposes to establish a devolved government for Cornwall with its own parliament or assembly that would have powers to make decisions on specific issues affecting the county. It's similar to the devolution arrangements already in place for Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, giving Cornwall more self-governance.

This bill aims to increase the powers that Wales has to govern itself by transferring certain decision-making powers from the UK Parliament to the Welsh Government and Welsh Parliament (Senedd Cymru). It's part of the ongoing process of devolution, which is about giving different parts of the UK more control over their own affairs.

This bill would require the UK government to hold a referendum asking Welsh people whether they support devolution - giving Wales greater independence to make its own decisions on things like health, education, and taxes. It's about letting Welsh citizens vote directly on how much self-government Wales should have.

The Great British Energy Act 2025 establishes a new state-owned energy company tasked with investing in renewable energy projects across the UK, particularly in wind, solar, and other clean energy infrastructure. The legislation aims to reduce the UK's dependence on fossil fuels, create jobs in the green energy sector, and help meet climate commitments. The bill grants the company powers to develop projects, form partnerships with private companies, and operate competitively within the energy market.

This bill aims to protect green belt land - the countryside and open spaces that surround UK towns and cities. It would strengthen the rules preventing developers from building on these areas, with the goal of keeping these green spaces available for nature, recreation, and preventing urban sprawl.

This bill aims to protect Green Belt land - designated countryside areas around towns and cities - from being developed into houses, shops, and factories. It would make the rules stricter to stop urban sprawl and keep these green spaces available for nature and public use.

This bill aims to create an official definition of 'green jobs' (work that helps the environment or tackles climate change) and introduce measures to encourage more people to work in these sectors. It's about making sure the UK has a clear strategy for developing environmentally-friendly careers as we move towards net zero emissions.

This bill updates a law from 1847 that sets out the rules for managing harbours, docks and piers in Britain. It modernises these rules so they work better for today's ports and shipping industry, rather than using 175-year-old regulations.

This bill aims to make hate crimes against people with learning difficulties and learning disabilities a specific criminal offence in law. Currently, such crimes may be prosecuted under general hate crime laws, but this bill would recognise disability-based hate crimes as a distinct crime category, similar to how race or religion-based hate crimes are already treated.

This Act establishes the position of National Data Guardian - an official person responsible for protecting people's health and social care information from misuse and breaches. They act as a guardian of your privacy in the NHS and care system, making sure your sensitive medical data is handled carefully.

This bill makes the role of the National Data Guardian - an independent official who protects patient privacy - stronger and more official. It gives them clear legal powers to check that hospitals, doctors, and health companies keep patient data secure and use it properly, rather than just advising them informally as they do now.

This Act introduces a new 'Health and Social Care Levy' - essentially a tax increase - to raise money specifically for the NHS and adult social care services. The tax is paid by employees and employers, and the money collected goes directly towards healthcare and care for older or vulnerable people.

This bill aims to improve public health across the UK by encouraging healthier lifestyles. It likely includes plans for health education campaigns, possibly stricter rules on certain products, or funding for health services - though the exact details aren't confirmed at this stage.

This bill aims to increase the number of families using the Healthy Start Scheme, a government programme that gives vouchers to low-income families with young children and pregnant women to buy nutritious food. It focuses on making the scheme easier to access and encouraging more eligible people to apply.

This bill would change the laws about hereditary titles in the UK so that daughters have the same rights as sons to inherit and pass on titles like Duke, Earl, or Baron. Currently, most titles follow 'male-only' inheritance rules that date back hundreds of years, meaning they often skip over daughters to go to sons or other male relatives.

This bill aims to control 'high cost credit' - loans with very high interest rates that can be expensive and risky for borrowers. It would set limits on interest rates and charges that lenders can apply, similar to existing rules for payday loans, to stop people being charged excessive amounts.

This bill aims to control how high-cost credit services (such as payday loan shops and pawn brokers) operate from physical shop premises. It would introduce new rules and regulations to make these services fairer and safer for customers, protecting people from predatory lending and extremely high interest rates.

This bill would require the government to regularly report to Parliament about the 'High Income Child Benefit Charge' - a rule that removes child benefit from families where one parent earns over £50,000 per year. The reports would show how this policy is actually affecting families, so politicians can see the real-world impact.

This bill asks the government to examine and evaluate the 'High Income Child Benefit Charge' - a rule that reduces or removes child benefit payments for families where one parent earns over £50,000 per year. The bill wants to understand how this charge affects families and whether it needs to be changed.

This bill allows the government to formally review and potentially adjust the spending and plans for the first phase of High Speed 2, the new high-speed railway being built in the UK. Essentially, it gives Parliament permission to reconsider how much money is being spent and what the project will actually deliver.

This bill allows the government to build a new high-speed railway line connecting Crewe to Manchester. It's part of the larger HS2 rail project and aims to provide faster train journeys between these cities, similar to how the existing high-speed rail works in other parts of the UK.

This Act gives the government permission to plan, build, and operate a new high-speed railway connecting London to Birmingham and the West Midlands. It allows the project to proceed and provides the legal framework needed to buy land, build the infrastructure, and run the trains.

This Act allows the government to prepare and plan for building a high-speed rail network in the UK. It gives permission for surveys, design work, and other preparation activities needed before actual construction can begin on new fast train routes.

This Act gives the government permission to build and operate a high-speed rail line connecting the West Midlands to Crewe in Cheshire. It allows the project to go ahead by setting out the legal framework for land use, construction, and running the new railway service.

This bill aims to limit advertisements for high-cost credit products (like payday loans that charge very high interest rates). It would control where and how these lenders can advertise to try to stop people, especially those who are struggling financially, from borrowing money at rates they might not be able to afford to repay.

This bill creates stricter electrical safety standards for high-rise residential buildings (tall apartment blocks). It requires better inspections of electrical wiring and equipment, and gives building owners clearer responsibilities to keep residents safe from electrical hazards.

This Act creates plans for the UK to build a Holocaust memorial - a permanent structure designed to remember the victims of the Holocaust and keep their memory alive for future generations. It shows the country's commitment to never forgetting this historical tragedy.

This bill would legally require local councils to keep a register of home-educated children and regularly check that they are receiving suitable education. Currently, parents can home-educate their children with less formal oversight, but this bill would give councils a clear responsibility to monitor home education in their area.

This bill establishes a mandatory registration system for home-educated children in the UK, requiring parents to notify local authorities of their intention to educate children at home and submit to regular monitoring. It aims to ensure home-schooled children receive adequate education and safeguarding oversight, similar to what schools provide. The bill also creates statutory duties for local authorities to support home educators with resources and guidance, and establishes minimum educational standards that must be met. It represents a significant shift toward greater state oversight of home education, which currently operates with minimal regulatory requirements.

This bill aims to make the honours system fairer by giving equal titles to all partners of people who receive honours. Currently, the rules mainly recognise married opposite-sex partners, but this bill would extend the same rights to same-sex partners and unmarried partners.

This bill would ban the sale of peat and peat-based products for gardening and horticulture purposes in the UK. Currently, gardeners and commercial growers can legally purchase peat to use in compost, potting soil, and soil conditioning. The bill aims to eliminate this market to protect peatland ecosystems, which store significant amounts of carbon and support rare wildlife. Gardeners would need to switch to alternative growing media such as coir, wood fibre, or compost made from green waste.

This bill requires the government to produce a comprehensive report on funding for hospices and health care services in the UK. The report must examine current funding levels, identify gaps between demand and available resources, and assess how well hospice services are financed across different regions. By mandating transparency and analysis of funding patterns, the bill aims to establish a clear evidence base for future policy decisions on end-of-life and palliative care provision.

The Hospices and Palliative Care Bill strengthens funding and regulation for hospice services and end-of-life care across the UK. It aims to ensure more consistent access to palliative care regardless of where patients live, establishes quality standards for hospice provision, and clarifies the legal framework for advance care planning and assisted dying decisions. The bill seeks to address the current patchwork of hospice funding and service availability, ensuring vulnerable patients receive dignified, compassionate care at the end of life.

This bill gives the government special priority to schedule debates and votes on Brexit-related laws in the House of Commons. Essentially, it allows the government to push Brexit business to the front of the queue ahead of other parliamentary business that MPs might want to discuss.

This Act gives the House of Commons Commission (the group that runs the day-to-day operations of Parliament) clearer legal powers to manage staff, facilities, and finances. It aims to make Parliament run more smoothly and ensure proper oversight of how it's managed.

This bill sets up or changes a financial fund specifically for House of Commons Members to access for work-related expenses and personal welfare support. It's essentially about creating a dedicated pot of money that MPs can use for certain approved purposes during their time in Parliament.

This bill proposes to amend (change) how the House of Lords operates. The exact changes aren't clear from the title alone, but it's designed to reform some aspect of the Lords - possibly how many members there are, how long they serve, or how they're chosen.

This bill stops the House of Lords from holding special elections (by-elections) to replace hereditary peers who die or step down. Currently, when a hereditary peer leaves, other hereditary peers vote to elect a replacement, this bill would end that practice, meaning fewer hereditary peers over time.

This bill would stop by-elections in the House of Lords when hereditary peers (people who inherit their seat through their family) leave or die. Currently, when one hereditary peer leaves, another from the same family group is elected to replace them. This bill would end that practice, gradually reducing the number of hereditary peers in the Lords.

This bill stops the House of Lords from holding by-elections to fill vacant seats left by hereditary peers. Currently, when a hereditary peer dies or retires, a special election is held to choose their replacement from other hereditary peers. This bill would end that practice, allowing seats to remain empty instead.

This bill would end by-elections in the House of Lords for hereditary peers (peers who inherit their title and seat). Currently, when a hereditary peer dies or leaves, a new one is elected to take their place. This bill would stop that process, gradually reducing the number of hereditary peers in Parliament.

This bill stops the House of Lords from holding by-elections when hereditary peers leave. Instead of replacing them, those seats would be eliminated, slowly reducing the number of hereditary peers in Parliament over time.

This bill would stop the House of Lords from holding by-elections when hereditary peers leave their positions. Currently, when a hereditary peer dies or resigns, other hereditary peers vote to elect a replacement; this bill would end that practice and let those seats stay empty.

This bill would stop the practice of holding by-elections to replace hereditary peers in the House of Lords when they leave. Currently, when a hereditary peer dies or retires, other hereditary peers vote to elect someone to take their place. This bill would end that process, meaning seats would stay empty.

This bill would reform how life peerages (the titles given to members of the House of Lords) are nominated and awarded in the UK. Currently, the Prime Minister has significant power to nominate peers, often as a reward for political loyalty or party donations. This bill would establish a more independent process, likely transferring some nomination power away from the Prime Minister to an independent or cross-party commission. The specific aim is to make peerage nominations more transparent and merit-based rather than politically influenced.

This bill proposes to change the House of Lords, which is the upper chamber of Parliament. The exact reforms aren't specified in this description, but they could include reducing the number of Lords members, changing how they're appointed, or introducing elections - the bill is still being debated so details may change.

This bill sets out new rules and standards for Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) - shared houses where several unrelated people rent rooms. It aims to make these homes safer and fairer for tenants by controlling things like overcrowding, safety standards, and landlord responsibilities.

This bill creates stricter regulations for Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) - homes rented out to several unrelated people. It aims to set minimum safety and housing standards, though the exact rules aren't yet clear as the bill is still being debated.

This bill requires Houses in Multiple Occupation to meet minimum energy efficiency standards (like proper insulation and heating) and requires landlords to provide Energy Performance Certificates showing how energy-efficient their properties are. It aims to make shared rental properties warmer, cheaper to heat, and better for the environment.

This bill aims to give local councils more power to make decisions about housing development and planning in their areas without as much interference from the national government. It's about shifting decision-making responsibility from Westminster to local communities, so they have more say in how their neighbourhoods change and develop.

This bill proposes changes to how housing is managed and built in the UK. The specific details of what reforms it includes would be found in the full bill text, but it's intended to address housing-related issues the government wants to fix.

This bill aims to establish and enforce basic housing standards for refugees and asylum seekers - people who have fled their home countries and are seeking protection in the UK. It ensures their temporary accommodation meets minimum requirements for safety, cleanliness, and living conditions.

This bill aims to change how the Human Rights Act 1998 defines a 'public authority' ,  the organisations that must respect people's human rights. Currently, courts decide case-by-case which organisations count; this bill would set clearer, fixed rules about which bodies must follow human rights law.

This bill changes how the Human Rights Act 1998 defines 'public authority' - basically, which organisations must follow human rights rules. Currently, this definition is unclear and causes arguments in court about whether private companies running public services (like hospitals or prisons) have to obey human rights law.

This bill aims to improve how the UK protects children who are victims of human trafficking - when criminals force children into dangerous situations like forced labour or sexual abuse. It likely introduces tougher penalties for traffickers, better support services for rescued children, and stronger ways to identify and stop trafficking before it happens.

This bill is about approving and supporting the Humber2100+ Project, which appears to be a long-term development or infrastructure plan for the Humber area (a region in England). The bill would give the project official parliamentary backing, though the full details of what the project involves aren't clear from the title alone.

This bill would make it illegal for UK citizens to import hunting trophies - things like animal heads, skins, or bones from animals they've hunted in other countries. The aim is to discourage trophy hunting of endangered and threatened species around the world.

This bill makes it a serious crime to enter or stay in the UK illegally, with punishments including prison time. It's designed to crack down on illegal immigration by making it a criminal matter rather than just an immigration issue, and to target people-smuggling gangs more harshly.

The Illegal Immigration (Offences) Bill creates new criminal offences and increases penalties related to illegal entry and residence in the UK. It aims to deter people from entering the country illegally by making it a specific crime to enter without permission, with sentences up to four years imprisonment. The bill also targets those who facilitate illegal immigration, including people smugglers and those assisting unauthorised entry. It strengthens enforcement powers for immigration officials and border authorities to detect, investigate, and prosecute immigration-related offences.

This bill creates new criminal offences for recording and sharing intimate images without consent. It makes it illegal to take, possess, or distribute sexually explicit photos or videos of someone without their permission, including 'deepfake' pornography created using AI. The legislation aims to protect people from sexual abuse and harassment, with penalties including fines and imprisonment. It covers both cases where images are shared maliciously and situations involving voyeurism or non-consensual filming.

This bill gives the UK government power to make its own immigration and social security rules now that it has left the EU. It removes EU immigration laws and changes how the UK handles benefits for people who move between the UK and EU countries. Essentially, it replaces EU rules with new UK-only rules.

This Act changes UK immigration and benefits rules after Brexit. It ends free movement from the EU, introduces a new points-based immigration system, and adjusts social security rules so they no longer follow EU law. Essentially, the UK now makes its own immigration decisions rather than sharing this power with Europe.

This bill would reduce or lower the tariffs (special taxes) that the UK charges on imported goods. The aim is to make foreign products cheaper when they enter the UK, but this could also affect UK-based businesses and workers in manufacturing industries.

This bill provides a mechanism for prisoners serving Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences to apply for re-sentencing, potentially reducing their prison terms. IPP sentences, abolished in 2012, were indeterminate sentences where prisoners had to prove they were safe to release rather than having a fixed release date. The bill aims to address the situation where hundreds of IPP prisoners remain incarcerated beyond what would have been their original tariff (minimum sentence length), many for decades, because they cannot satisfy increasingly difficult release criteria.

This bill would change who gets to pick the Independent Adviser on Ministers' Interests - the person who checks whether government ministers are following the rules about conflicts of interest. Instead of the Prime Minister choosing them, Parliament would make the choice instead.

This bill changes how the Anti-slavery Commissioner is appointed. Instead of the government choosing them, Parliament would select them. The Anti-slavery Commissioner is an official who investigates slavery and human trafficking in the UK and pushes for stronger action to stop it.

The Industry and Exports (Financial Assistance) Act 2026 enables the UK government to provide financial support to domestic industries and businesses seeking to expand into export markets. This includes grants, loans, and guarantees designed to help companies compete internationally and strengthen UK manufacturing and services sectors. The act establishes the legal framework and funding mechanisms for these assistance programmes, allowing government departments to deploy capital directly to eligible businesses. It aims to boost economic growth, create jobs, and improve the UK's trade position post-Brexit.

This bill would change UK inheritance law so that unmarried couples living together long-term can inherit from each other's property and money when one dies, even if there's no will. Currently, only married couples and civil partners have these automatic inheritance rights; cohabitants have no legal claim unless a will is made.

This bill creates an official, legal definition of what the UK means by 'International Development Assistance' - essentially setting clear rules about what types of spending count as foreign aid. This helps Parliament and the public understand and monitor where this money goes and ensures it's genuinely helping developing countries.

This Act allows the UK to legally support and participate in the Special Court for Sierra Leone, an international tribunal that prosecutes those responsible for serious crimes during Sierra Leone's brutal 1991-2002 civil war. It gives the UK the power to help investigate, prosecute, and support the court's work to bring those responsible to justice.

This bill proposes new government regulations for internet platforms and messaging services to protect users from harmful content and ensure companies are more accountable. It would set rules about how platforms moderate content, protect children online, and make their decision-making processes clearer to users.

This Act gives UK security and police services legal permission to collect and access people's communications data (like phone records and internet history) to investigate serious crimes and terrorism. It requires warrants and oversight, but creates a framework for large-scale surveillance activities.

This bill aims to make investment managers follow clearer and stricter rules about protecting the money they manage for clients. It strengthens 'fiduciary duties' - meaning investment managers must legally prioritize their clients' best interests rather than their own profits.

This bill proposes to set up a second official investigation into the 2003 Iraq War and how the UK government made decisions to join it. The goal would be to produce a public report examining what went wrong and holding decision-makers accountable for their actions.

This bill would make it illegal for the UK to sell weapons and military equipment to Israel. It's a response to concerns about how weapons are used in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and represents one side of a major debate about whether the UK should restrict arms exports based on human rights concerns.

This bill asks Parliament to investigate the idea of a 'jobs guarantee' - a scheme where the government would offer a job to anyone who wants one but can't find work. The bill doesn't create the scheme itself, but instead funds research to understand if it's a good idea and how it could be set up.

This bill asks Parliament to fund research into a 'Jobs Guarantee Scheme' - a potential policy where the government would offer a job to anyone who wants one. The bill doesn't create the scheme itself, but instead investigates whether it could work in practice and what it would involve.

This Act changes the rules around judicial review - the process where courts check if the government has acted fairly and legally. It introduces stricter time limits for bringing cases to court, makes some cases harder to challenge, and adjusts how the courts handle legal fees and appeals.

This bill allows Kew Gardens to manage and lease its property more independently, rather than needing Parliament's approval for lease decisions. It's designed to give the organization more control over how it uses its land and buildings to support its work as a world-renowned botanical research and education center.

This bill aims to improve support for kinship care - when children are raised by relatives instead of their parents. It would likely provide better funding, clearer legal rights, and more help for these family carers so children in their care have stable, secure homes.

This bill would introduce a Land Value Tax - a new way of taxing people based on the value of the land they own, separate from any buildings on it. The idea is to raise money for the government and discourage land from being left unused in valuable areas.

This bill aims to regulate laser pens by introducing new rules around their sale, ownership, and use in the UK. It would likely set age limits for buying them, restrict who can own them, and set rules for how they can be used - similar to how other potentially dangerous items are currently controlled.

This bill proposes to ban the use of lead ammunition in the UK. Lead bullets can contaminate soil and water, and may harm wildlife and people who eat game shot with lead ammunition. The bill would require hunters and sport shooters to use non-lead alternatives instead.

This bill aims to make leasehold fairer by giving leaseholders (long-term renters) more power and cheaper costs. It could make it easier to extend leases, reduce ground rent charges, and give leaseholders more say in how their buildings are run and maintained.

This bill aims to protect leaseholders (people who rent their homes long-term) by making rules about insurance costs and commission fees. It would require property companies to be transparent about how much they're charging and why, stopping them from secretly marking up prices on things like buildings insurance.

This bill aims to reform the rules around 'forfeiture' - the process where a landlord can take back a leasehold property if a tenant breaks their lease agreement, usually by not paying rent. The bill would likely make this process fairer for leaseholders by giving them more protection and opportunities to fix problems before losing their home.

This bill aims to help leaseholders (people who rent flats long-term) by making it clearer and easier for them to challenge service charges that seem unreasonably high. Service charges pay for building maintenance like repairs and cleaning, but some leaseholders feel they're being overcharged, so this bill would strengthen their ability to question these costs.

This bill aims to help leaseholders who believe a tribunal (a type of court) has made an unfair decision. It would let them challenge that decision more easily and recover money they spent on lawyers if their challenge succeeds. The bill tries to make the system fairer for people renting their homes long-term.

This bill reforms the leasehold system specifically for integrated retirement communities, developments where older residents live in self-contained homes or apartments with shared facilities and care services. It addresses issues where residents face unfair lease terms, excessive ground rents, and limited rights to extend or manage their leases. The bill aims to give retirement community residents stronger protections, fairer financial terms, and greater control over their living arrangements, similar to protections already offered to other leaseholders in the broader leasehold reform agenda.

This Act gives Leeds City Council specific legal powers to manage certain aspects of the city. It's a local law that allows the council to do things like borrow money, manage land and buildings, and run services in ways that work best for Leeds rather than following one-size-fits-all national rules.

The Legal Services Act reforms how lawyers and law firms are regulated in the UK. It opens up the legal profession to new ways of working (like non-lawyer ownership) and creates an independent regulator to oversee quality and protect consumers.

This bill would make it legal for doctors to prescribe cannabis-based medicines to patients who need them for medical treatment. Currently, cannabis is illegal in the UK, so this would change the law to allow medicinal use only, not recreational use.

The Licensing Hours Extensions Act 2026 allows local licensing authorities in the UK to grant extensions to operating hours for alcohol-serving establishments such as pubs, bars, and nightclubs beyond their current standard closing times. The bill gives premises greater flexibility to apply for later closing times, subject to local council approval and consideration of factors like public nuisance and crime prevention. It represents a shift towards deregulation, allowing market demand and local decision-making to determine trading hours rather than strict national restrictions.

This bill proposes to give lip-reading an official status in UK law, probably by setting quality standards, requiring proper training, or establishing it as a recognized profession. It aims to improve communication access for people who are deaf or hard of hearing, ensuring they receive consistent, reliable support when lip-reading is used.

This bill amends the classification and regulatory framework for Listed Investment Companies (LICs) in the UK. It modifies how these companies, which are closed-end funds traded on stock exchanges, are categorized and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). The bill aims to provide greater flexibility for LICs in their operations and investment strategies while clarifying their legal status. Key measures include changing how LICs are classified under FCA rules and potentially reducing certain regulatory burdens that apply to them.

This bill establishes mandatory safety standards and regulatory requirements for lithium-ion batteries used in consumer products, energy storage systems, and vehicles across the UK. It requires manufacturers to conduct safety testing, include safety labelling and documentation, and implement recall procedures for defective batteries. The bill also creates enforcement powers for regulators to inspect facilities, issue penalties for non-compliance, and sets standards for battery recycling and disposal to prevent fires and environmental contamination. The legislation aims to reduce incidents of battery fires, explosions, and toxic releases that have increased significantly with the growth in lithium-ion battery use.

This bill creates new safety and environmental rules for large facilities that store lithium-ion batteries. It aims to reduce the risk of fires at these storage sites and protect the environment by requiring better safety systems and proper environmental permits before these facilities can operate.

The Live Music Act 2012 simplifies the rules around hosting live music in smaller venues. It removes some licensing requirements and fees for small-scale performances (like acoustic sets in pubs), making it cheaper and easier for communities to enjoy live music without dealing with lots of government paperwork.

The Living Wage (Reporting) Bill requires large employers to publicly disclose information about how many of their employees earn below the Living Wage threshold and what proportion of their workforce this represents. The bill aims to increase transparency around low-wage employment and create public accountability for companies. By making this data publicly available, the legislation seeks to encourage employers to improve pay standards and allow consumers and investors to make informed decisions based on companies' wage practices.

This bill gives local councils in England greater powers to plan, control, and improve transport services in their areas. Currently, many transport decisions are made by central government; this bill would shift more responsibility and decision-making power to local level, allowing communities to shape their own transport systems.

This bill requires local authorities (councils) to protect wildlife on the roads they maintain and repair. It aims to reduce the number of animals killed or injured by traffic by giving councils new powers and responsibilities to implement wildlife-friendly measures on local roads.

This bill would require local councils to create and regularly update Infrastructure Requirement Plans - detailed documents setting out what roads, schools, hospitals, utilities and other services their area will need over the next 10-15 years. The goal is to make sure communities have better planning for future growth and investment.

This bill gives local councils in England more control over religious observances at their official events and ceremonies. Instead of following strict national rules, each council could decide how to handle prayers, religious symbols, and other faith-related elements at council meetings and public events.

The Local Government and Elections Bill reforms how local councils operate and hold elections across England. It introduces measures to strengthen council leadership through directly elected mayors in certain areas, requires councils to publish more financial information and performance data, and changes electoral arrangements including moving to all-out elections on a four-yearly cycle in some councils. The bill aims to increase transparency, improve accountability, and modernize local government structures.

This bill regulates how local authorities can place looked-after children (children in care) in residential placements far from their home area. It sets rules about distance thresholds, consultation requirements, and safeguarding measures when councils place children in care homes or foster placements outside their local region. The bill aims to keep children closer to their families, schools, and support networks while ensuring proper oversight when distant placements are necessary. It introduces new duties for local authorities to justify and monitor these placements.

The Lord Advocate Bill addresses the constitutional role and independence of Scotland's Lord Advocate, who serves as the country's chief law officer and head of the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service. The bill aims to clarify the Lord Advocate's position within Scotland's devolved government, particularly regarding their prosecutorial independence and accountability arrangements. It establishes clearer separation between the Lord Advocate's role as a government minister and their duty to act impartially in criminal prosecutions. The reforms seek to strengthen protections for prosecutorial decision-making from political interference while defining how the Lord Advocate answers to Parliament.

This bill makes changes to the Lords Spiritual - the Church of England bishops who sit in the House of Lords. The exact changes aren't yet clear, but the bill aims to update how these religious representatives participate in Parliament.

This Act allows female bishops of the Church of England to become members of the House of Lords automatically, in the same way senior male bishops have been able to for centuries. Before this law, only male bishops could hold these positions, so it removed a gender-based barrier.

This bill aims to encourage UK homes to switch from traditional gas boilers to low-carbon heating methods, such as heat pumps powered by electricity. It's designed to help reduce greenhouse gas emissions and fight climate change, though it affects how people heat their homes and hot water.

This bill would allow certain low-risk workplaces to skip formal risk assessments (detailed safety checks). It assumes some jobs are so safe that they don't need the usual safety paperwork requirements, though they'd still need to follow basic health and safety laws.

This bill proposes to ban letter boxes that are installed at low levels on buildings. The exact reasons aren't clear from the title alone, but such a law would make it illegal to have these low-level letter boxes and could require people to install them higher up instead.

This Act sets out the legal framework for how Manchester City Council operates and what powers it has to run the city. It covers things like decision-making, budgets, and how the council should serve the people of Manchester.

This bill changes the rules for how the Marine Accident Investigation Branch - the UK government body that investigates shipping accidents - publishes and manages its investigation reports. It's currently at the stage where MPs debate whether the bill is a good idea before voting on the specific details.

This bill aims to create a licensing system for activities in UK marine waters (at sea). It would require certain sea-based activities to get official permission from the government, similar to how you need a license to drive a car. This helps the government manage what happens in UK waters and aims to balance business, environmental protection, and public safety.

This bill would ban or restrict bottom trawling, a fishing method where heavy nets are dragged along the seabed, within Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) in English waters. Bottom trawling disrupts seabed habitats, damages ecosystems, and can destroy marine life and fish breeding grounds. The bill aims to strengthen environmental protections in designated marine conservation zones by preventing this damaging fishing practice in these sensitive areas. It represents a targeted approach to protecting England's marine biodiversity without necessarily banning the practice in non-protected waters.

This bill would allow secular (non-religious) belief organisations to officially conduct legal marriages. Currently, only religious organisations and registrars can do this. The bill would give humanist groups and similar organisations the same legal power to marry couples, recognising that some people want meaningful ceremonies that reflect their non-religious beliefs.

This Act changed UK law to allow same-sex couples to get married legally. Before 2013, only opposite-sex couples could marry. The Act made marriage equal for everyone, regardless of whether someone is attracted to the same sex or opposite sex. It gave same-sex married couples the same legal rights and responsibilities as other married couples.

This bill would make it legal for same-sex couples (gay and lesbian couples) to get married in Northern Ireland. Currently, same-sex marriage is already legal in England, Scotland, and Wales, but Northern Ireland has different laws. This bill would bring Northern Ireland into line with the rest of the UK.

This bill would allow same-sex couples to legally marry in Northern Ireland. Currently, only different-sex couples can marry there, even though same-sex marriage is already legal in the rest of the UK. The bill would update Northern Ireland's marriage laws to match the rest of Britain.

This bill would extend same-sex marriage rights to British overseas territories that don't currently allow it. Currently, same-sex couples can marry in the UK, but some of Britain's overseas territories still ban it. The bill would change this by requiring those territories to recognize same-sex marriage as legal.

This bill proposes to make changes to the Marriage Act 1949, which is the main law controlling how marriages work in the UK. However, without knowing the specific amendments being proposed, it's difficult to say exactly what will change - you would need to read the bill's detailed proposals to understand what new rules it would introduce.

This bill proposes to amend (change) the Marriage Act 1949, which is the main law controlling how marriages work in the UK. The exact changes aren't specified in this basic information, but the bill aims to update these 75-year-old rules for modern times. It's currently at an early stage and hasn't been debated in detail yet.

This bill proposes setting a maximum wage, a legal limit on how much money the highest-paid people in the UK can earn. The exact wage limit isn't specified in this description, but the bill would prevent earnings above that threshold.

This bill requires meat producers and retailers to provide clear information to consumers about how animals were killed during the slaughter process. The labelling would indicate whether animals were stunned before slaughter (and the method used) or killed without pre-stunning, as permitted under religious exemptions. The aim is to give UK consumers transparent information about production methods when purchasing meat products, enabling them to make informed choices based on animal welfare considerations.

This bill aims to make it easier for doctors to use new and experimental medical treatments for patients in life-threatening situations where conventional treatments haven't worked. It tries to balance patient safety with giving patients hope of accessing innovative therapies more quickly than the usual approval process would allow.

This bill proposes to stop Members of Parliament from having second jobs while they are serving as MPs. It would force MPs to choose between being a full-time politician or working in another profession, but not doing both at the same time.

This Act changes the rules about who can approve important mental health decisions in the UK's healthcare system. It transfers some approval powers from central bodies to senior mental health professionals, aiming to speed up decision-making for patients who need mental health treatment or care.

This bill requires the UK government to issue formal travel advice warning British citizens about the risk of methanol poisoning in specific countries or regions where contaminated alcohol has caused deaths or serious illness. The bill aims to ensure that tourists and travellers have clear, accessible information about which destinations have experienced methanol-poisoning incidents, helping them make informed decisions about where to drink alcohol abroad. It places a duty on the Foreign Office to update this advice regularly and ensure warnings are prominently displayed in travel guidance. The bill responds to cases where British travellers have died or been seriously harmed after consuming illegally-produced or contaminated alcoholic drinks in destinations where such poisoning is a known hazard.

This bill updates the official definition of 'microgeneration' - small renewable energy systems like solar panels or wind turbines that homeowners install themselves. By changing what counts as microgeneration, it aims to help more people benefit from government support for renewable energy and encourage more people to generate their own green energy.

This bill aims to encourage 'microgeneration' - when homes and local communities produce their own small amounts of renewable energy. It would likely remove barriers that currently make this difficult and could include support or incentives to help people install solar panels, small wind turbines, or other renewable energy equipment.

This bill would legally require washing machines sold in the UK to have built-in filters that trap microplastics (tiny plastic fibres from synthetic clothing) so they don't escape into the water system and harm marine life and the environment.

This bill sets minimum energy performance standards for buildings across the UK. It requires buildings to become more energy-efficient by improving things like insulation and heating systems, which should reduce energy bills and help meet the UK's climate goals.
