It aims to create a consistent process for deciding which areas deserve this special status and what rules should protect them.

This Act reforms how post-16 education and skills training work in England. It changes the system so colleges and training providers focus more on what employers need, helps young people choose between academic and practical routes, and aims to get more people into work-ready skills.

This bill aims to make it easier for small and medium-sized co-operatives to develop and grow. Co-operatives are businesses owned by their workers or members who share the profits and decisions. The bill would likely provide financial help, advice, and other support to help these types of businesses succeed.

This bill creates a 'Social Energy Tariff' - a scheme that gives discounted gas and electricity rates to people who are struggling to afford energy bills. It aims to help vulnerable households keep their homes warm and powered at a lower cost.

This bill would set up a new government commission to examine social justice issues - things like poverty, discrimination, and unfairness in society. The commission would study these problems and suggest ways to make society fairer, though it would not have direct power to make changes itself.

The Social Media (Access to Accounts) Bill would require social media companies to provide law enforcement and other authorised bodies with access to user accounts and data during investigations. The bill aims to give police and security services tools to investigate crimes such as child exploitation, terrorism, and organised crime by requiring platforms to decrypt or provide access to encrypted messages and account information. It would establish a legal framework requiring companies to comply with access requests, with penalties for non-compliance. Essentially, it creates a backdoor into encrypted social media platforms for law enforcement purposes.

This bill would require social media platforms (like Instagram, TikTok, and X) to verify users' real identities before they can create accounts or post. Instead of using made-up names, people would need to prove who they actually are, similar to opening a bank account.

This Act allows the government to give one-off extra payments to people receiving social security benefits (like Universal Credit or pension credit). It was designed to help people cope with rising living costs, particularly during the cost of living crisis in 2022.

This Act allows the government to make one-off or temporary extra payments to people receiving certain social security benefits. It's designed to provide financial support to households facing difficulty, particularly during periods of economic hardship.

This bill states that the UK Parliament is the supreme law-making body and cannot be overruled by the European Communities (now known as the European Union). It reasserts parliamentary sovereignty, meaning MPs have final say over UK law rather than any outside authority.

The Space Industry (Indemnities) Act 2025 allows the UK government to provide legal indemnity (financial protection from liability) to commercial space companies operating in Britain. This means the government will cover costs if a space company causes damage, such as harm to people, property, or the environment, during launch, orbital operations, or re-entry activities. The Act enables the UK space sector to compete globally by reducing the insurance burden on companies, while establishing a framework for when and how government protection applies. Essentially, British taxpayers assume some financial risk so that UK space businesses can operate more cheaply and attract investment.

This bill would create a new government role - a Special Envoy - whose job is to protect and promote freedom of religion and belief in the UK and abroad. The envoy would help ensure people aren't discriminated against because of their religion or beliefs, and would advise the government on these issues.

This Act gives St. Austell Market specific legal powers and rules to operate as a market in Cornwall. It sets out how the market should be managed and what authority it has to run its day-to-day business.

The State Actors (Proscription) Bill would allow the UK government to formally ban and designate foreign state actors, such as governments, their agents, or state-controlled organizations, as threats to national security, similar to how terrorist organizations are currently proscribed. Once proscribed, it would become illegal to support, fund, or work with these entities, with criminal penalties for violations. The bill aims to give the UK stronger legal tools to counter hostile state activities like espionage, disinformation campaigns, and political interference without requiring a full diplomatic break or waiting for individual crimes to be prosecuted.

This bill establishes a national oversight mechanism to investigate and review deaths that occur in state custody or involving state agents (such as police, prisons, or armed forces). It creates independent scrutiny of how these deaths are handled, aims to improve transparency in investigations, and establishes clear procedures and accountability standards across the UK. The mechanism would ensure consistent investigation practices and enable families to access information about state-related deaths more effectively.

This bill aims to clarify what type of worker someone is (employee, self-employed, or something in between) and ensure they get the rights and protections they deserve. It's designed to tackle situations where people work like employees but don't get employee benefits.

This bill aims to clarify and improve the legal status of different types of workers in the UK. It would likely change how workers are classified (employee, worker, or self-employed) to make sure people get fair treatment, proper pay, and workplace protections based on the type of work they actually do.

This bill requires the UK government to commission and publish a report examining whether Statutory Adoption Pay (SAP) should be extended to self-employed workers. Currently, only employees receive the statutory entitlement to paid leave when adopting a child; self-employed parents receive nothing. The bill does not directly extend SAP itself, but instead mandates that ministers investigate the feasibility, costs, and implications of doing so, and then present their findings to Parliament within a specified timeframe.

This bill modifies the procedures for how statutory instruments (detailed laws made by government ministers under powers granted by Parliament) are created, scrutinised, and implemented. Statutory instruments are a fast-track form of legislation used thousands of times yearly for everything from setting benefit rates to environmental regulations. The bill aims to improve parliamentary oversight of these instruments, though the specific amendments would depend on the bill's current provisions in the House of Lords.

The Steel Industry (Special Measures) Act introduces targeted government interventions to support the UK steel sector during a period of economic challenge. The bill likely includes provisions such as subsidies, tax relief, or preferential purchasing agreements for UK steel producers, and may establish a regulatory framework to protect domestic manufacturers from unfair foreign competition. These measures aim to preserve steel-making capacity, protect jobs in steel communities, and maintain the UK's industrial base. The act represents a direct government commitment to prevent further closures of steel plants and maintain supply chains critical to other UK industries.

This bill aims to stop what's called 'SLAPP' (Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation) - where wealthy people or companies use expensive court cases to scare ordinary people into silence for speaking out or campaigning. The bill would create new protections to dismiss these cases early, saving people money and protecting their right to speak up without fear.

This bill aims to stop 'SLAPP suits' - expensive legal cases filed mainly to intimidate and silence critics rather than to win in court. It would give courts the power to quickly dismiss these cases and protect campaigners, journalists, and ordinary people who speak out on matters of public interest.

This bill aims to stop 'SLAPP' lawsuits (Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation) - cases filed mainly to scare people into staying quiet rather than to win in court. It would give judges the power to throw out such cases early and protect people's right to speak up about matters of public interest without fear of crippling legal bills.

This bill proposes to update the old rules about how noble titles (peerages and baronetcies) are inherited when someone dies. It aims to modernise the system so it works better for today's society, rather than following centuries-old traditions that may no longer make sense.

This bill aims to tackle high sugar consumption in the UK by requiring companies to reduce sugar in their products, making nutrition labels clearer and easier to understand, and controlling how sugary foods and drinks are advertised. The goal is to help people make healthier choices and reduce obesity-related health problems.

This Act temporarily relaxed Sunday trading laws in London during the 2012 Olympic and Paralympic Games, allowing large shops to open for longer than the usual 6-hour limit. It was a one-off measure to help businesses and make shopping easier during the Games period.

The Superannuation Act 2010 reformed the pension schemes for public sector employees in the UK. It changed how much workers and the government contribute to pensions, increased retirement ages, and tied pension increases to inflation, aiming to control long-term government spending on pensions.

This Act allows the UK government to spend money on day-to-day services before the full annual budget (Supply) is officially approved by Parliament. It's a temporary measure to keep the country running, and also makes adjustments to previously approved spending limits when needed.

This Act is Parliament's formal approval of how the government will spend billions of pounds across different departments and public services for one year. It's essentially the government's annual budget - deciding which services get how much money to function.

This Act gives the government official permission to spend a set amount of money on various public services and departments during 2012-13. It's a routine annual law that authorises the government's budget, similar to a household deciding how much to spend on different bills and expenses each year.

This Act allows the government to spend the money it has set aside for running public services during 2017-18. It's like a family approving their budget, Parliament agrees on how much money each government department can spend that year.

This bill authorizes the government to spend money from the public purse for the financial year 2024-25. It approves the 'Main Estimates', detailed spending plans submitted by each government department, allowing them to access funds for operations like the NHS, defence, education, and welfare. Without this annual bill, government departments would be unable to legally spend taxpayers' money. The bill also sets limits on how much each department can borrow if needed.

This bill authorizes the government to spend money from the UK Treasury for the financial year 2025-26 based on departmental spending plans (Main Estimates). It formally approves how much money each government department, including Health, Defence, Education, and others, can spend on their operations and services. Without this annual bill, the government cannot legally access public funds. The bill also allows the Treasury to make minor adjustments to spending allocations if circumstances change during the year.

This bill would make it a more serious crime for adults to supply or sell drugs to children under 16. It creates an 'aggravated offence' - a category with tougher penalties - specifically for drug supply to young people, going beyond standard drug supply laws.

This bill aims to create stronger protections for elderly people and at-risk adults by improving how abuse is reported, investigated, and prevented. It would likely set out clearer rules for care providers, social services, and other organizations about spotting warning signs and taking action when someone may be being harmed.

This bill aims to make sure that parents and carers can easily find accurate information about support available to them and their babies - such as healthcare services, benefits, and parenting advice. Currently, this information is scattered across different websites and organisations, so the bill would require better coordination to help families get the help they need.

The Sustainable Aviation Fuel Act 2026 establishes requirements for UK airlines and fuel suppliers to gradually increase their use of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), jet fuel produced from renewable sources like used cooking oil, agricultural waste, or synthetic processes, rather than conventional fossil fuels. The bill sets binding blending mandates, requiring a percentage of all jet fuel used in UK aviation to be SAF, with targets increasing year-on-year. It also includes investment incentives for SAF production facilities in the UK and establishes certification standards to ensure environmental credibility. The aim is to reduce aviation's carbon emissions while building a domestic SAF industry.

The Sustainable Communities Act 2007 aims to help create neighbourhoods where people can live, work, and thrive long-term. It gives local communities and councils more say in planning their own areas, focusing on making places better for residents through improved housing, jobs, and services.

This bill gives local councils (in England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland) more responsibility for approving and planning sustainable energy projects in their areas. It aims to speed up decision-making on renewable energy by letting communities have a stronger voice in how solar, wind, and other clean energy developments happen near them.

This bill requires the government to systematically evaluate whether tax reliefs (tax breaks given to specific industries, activities, or groups) actually deliver their intended economic and social benefits. Currently, many tax reliefs exist without rigorous assessment of their effectiveness or value for money. The bill establishes a framework for regular review and evidence-gathering on tax reliefs, enabling Parliament to make better-informed decisions about which reliefs to maintain, modify, or remove.

This bill would establish an annual 'Taxation Freedom Day' - a date showing the point in the year when British workers have earned enough to pay all their taxes. It aims to make people more aware of their total tax burden by calculating when their earnings stop going to taxes and start being their own money.

This Act reforms technical and further education in England to make it more practical and work-focused. It encourages new types of qualifications and training programmes that teach real job skills, while trying to improve how colleges, employers, and training providers work together.

This Act makes it simpler for telecoms companies to install broadband and phone infrastructure (cables and equipment) in leasehold properties (flats and shared buildings) without needing permission from every single leaseholder. It speeds up getting high-speed internet to more people, but gives property owners less control over their buildings.

The Terminal Illness (Relief of Pain) Bill would allow doctors to provide pain relief medication to terminally ill patients, even when such treatment might inadvertently shorten life as a side effect. The bill aims to clarify legal protections for medical professionals who prioritize symptom relief and comfort care in end-of-life situations. It establishes that doctors acting in good faith to alleviate severe suffering are not committing a criminal act, even if high-dose pain medication hastens death. The legislation focuses on palliative care rather than actively ending life.

This bill aims to improve the rights and support available to people who have been told they are dying from an illness. It would likely include things like better access to palliative care (pain relief and comfort care), clearer legal rights, and support for families during end-of-life care.

This bill would allow adults in England who are terminally ill and expected to die within six months to request and self-administer life-ending medication, subject to strict safeguards. Two doctors would need to independently confirm the person meets eligibility criteria, including a 14-day waiting period between requests. The bill aims to give terminally ill people greater autonomy over their end-of-life choices while including protections against coercion and ensuring only those with full mental capacity can access this option.

The Terrorism (Protection of Premises) Act establishes legal requirements for owners and operators of certain buildings and public spaces to implement security measures against terrorist attacks. The act defines which premises must comply (typically high-risk locations like transport hubs, shopping centres, and government buildings) and sets out duties for assessing vulnerabilities, installing protective infrastructure, and training staff. Premises that fail to meet these standards can face penalties, and the act grants authorities power to issue improvement notices where security is deemed inadequate. The legislation aims to reduce casualties and prevent attacks by making it harder for terrorists to exploit vulnerable locations.

This Act prevents people convicted of terrorist offences from being released early on licence (a type of conditional release). Instead of potentially leaving prison after serving two-thirds of their sentence, terrorist offenders must now serve at least three-quarters of their full sentence before they can be considered for release.

This bill allows police to issue on-the-spot fines to people caught shoplifting, rather than always taking them to court. It's designed to be quicker and easier than the current court process, but still hold shoplifters responsible for their actions.

This bill aims to increase criminal penalties for stealing tools and equipment used by tradespeople in their work. Currently, theft is sentenced based on the item's monetary value, which often results in low sentences for stolen tools despite their critical importance to workers' livelihoods. The bill proposes that courts should treat tool theft more seriously, potentially as a specific offense category, to reflect the disproportionate harm caused when self-employed tradespeople lose their equipment and cannot work. This would result in harsher sentences than standard theft charges.

This bill aims to make it easier for British people, including journalists and officials, to visit and work in Tibet. It does this by requiring the UK government to negotiate with China for reciprocal (equal two-way) access, rather than accepting restrictions on who can travel there.

This bill aims to increase British access to Tibet and Xinjiang by making it a 'two-way street' - the UK would only allow Chinese officials equal access to Britain if China allows British people the same freedom to visit, work, and investigate in these regions. It's designed to challenge restrictions the Chinese government currently places on foreign visitors and journalists in these areas.

This bill creates a code of practice for 'tied pubs' - pubs where the landlord must buy beer from a specific brewery company that owns the building. It aims to protect pub landlords from unfair treatment by setting out clear rules about rent prices, maintenance responsibilities, and how complaints are dealt with.

This bill aims to reduce smoking and vaping, especially among young people, by introducing stricter rules around how tobacco and vapes are sold, advertised, and who can buy them. It's designed as a long-term public health measure to make these products less accessible and appealing to teenagers.

This bill makes tobacco manufacturers responsible for managing the waste their products create, including discarded cigarette butts and packaging. Companies would need to fund clean-up schemes and support smoking reduction efforts, rather than leaving these costs to taxpayers and local councils.

This bill changes the planning rules for electricity-generating facilities to make it quicker and easier to get approval for building them. Currently, many energy projects need detailed planning permission; this bill would reduce those requirements so renewable energy can be built faster across the UK.

This bill changes the planning rules for electricity-generating projects in England. It aims to speed up the process of building new power generation facilities by reducing the amount of planning permission needed, so energy projects can be developed more quickly than they can under current law.

This bill extends concessionary travel schemes operated by Transport for London (TfL), likely expanding eligibility criteria or geographic coverage for reduced-fare passes. The bill aims to make public transport more affordable for specific groups, potentially including older people, disabled passengers, young people, or low-income Londoners. By extending these concessions, the bill seeks to increase accessibility to the London transport network while managing the financial impact on TfL's budget.

This Act establishes the UK Infrastructure Bank, a government-backed organisation that lends money and provides investment to support major infrastructure projects. It aims to help build and improve essential services like transport, energy, and internet across the UK.

This bill would place a legal duty on the UK Government to negotiate and pursue membership in a customs union with the European Union. Rather than leaving the customs arrangements as they currently stand, the bill would require ministers to actively seek negotiations with the EU aimed at establishing closer trade ties through a formal customs union. The bill effectively mandates that the Government must attempt to rejoin or create a customs union framework with EU partners, rather than maintaining the current post-Brexit separate customs status.

This bill aims to make sure unaccompanied asylum-seeking children get proper legal advice and support when appealing asylum decisions. Currently, some children struggle to understand the complex legal system and may not have access to lawyers. The bill would help ensure they have fair representation to present their cases properly.

This bill makes it a criminal offence to enter a football stadium without authorisation (like a valid ticket or permission). It aims to tackle problems like gate-crashing, hooliganism, and safety issues at football matches by giving police stronger powers to prevent and punish unauthorised entry.

The Unauthorised Entry to Football Matches Act 2026 creates new criminal offences and enforcement powers to prevent people from entering football stadiums without valid tickets or permission. The bill strengthens penalties for pitch invasions, unauthorised entry, and re-entry after being banned from a venue. It gives football clubs and stewards expanded powers to eject individuals and introduces measures to tackle ticket touting and fraudulent ticket use. The legislation aims to improve stadium safety, protect paying supporters' experience, and reduce disruption at matches.

This bill aims to make it illegal for businesses to engage in 'unconscionable conduct' - meaning behaviour that is so unfair, dishonest or exploitative that it shocks the conscience. It would give customers and small businesses new legal powers to challenge and get compensation from companies that treat them this way.

This bill would create exceptions to the under-occupancy penalty, which reduces housing benefits for people in council homes with spare bedrooms. It would allow certain vulnerable people or groups to keep their full housing support even if their homes are considered too large for their household size.

This bill asks the government to carry out and publish a detailed report on the under-occupancy penalty (commonly called the 'bedroom tax'). This is the rule that reduces housing benefits for people in social housing who have spare bedrooms. The bill simply demands information and transparency, it doesn't change the policy itself, just investigates its effects.

This bill would require Parliament to commission and publish a report investigating the 'under-occupancy penalty' (commonly called the bedroom tax). This is a policy that reduces housing benefit payments for people in social housing who have more bedrooms than the government thinks they need. The report would examine the impact of this policy on people and families.

This bill asks Parliament to produce a detailed report examining the under-occupancy penalty - a rule that reduces housing benefits for people on low incomes who have 'spare' bedrooms. It's not trying to change the law itself, just to gather and publish information about how the policy is actually working.

This bill proposes creating an official UK Register of Places - basically a comprehensive list of important locations across the country. The register would record details about these places and could be used by the government, councils, and the public for planning, historical records, and other purposes.

This bill would establish new UK parliamentary oversight mechanisms for United States military and security operations conducted on British territory or involving British personnel. It would require the US military to provide advance notice to Parliament of certain operations, grant Parliament rights to review classified agreements, and potentially allow the UK to restrict or withdraw consent for specific US activities. The bill aims to strengthen parliamentary scrutiny of the US-UK military relationship and ensure UK sovereignty over decisions affecting British soil and citizens.

The Universal Credit Act 2025 is a legislative framework governing the UK's main welfare benefit system that consolidates and modernises rules for how Universal Credit operates. The bill likely addresses administration, eligibility criteria, payment structures, and work incentives within the existing Universal Credit scheme. It would establish the statutory basis for recent policy changes and set out the government's approach to supporting working-age people, unemployed individuals, and those with reduced work capacity. The Act aims to clarify the legal framework within which Universal Credit is delivered.

This bill proposes to restrict Universal Credit eligibility to British citizens only, excluding non-British nationals (including EU citizens post-Brexit, other foreign nationals, and potentially asylum seekers or visa holders). The measure aims to reduce welfare spending on non-citizen residents and prioritise support for British citizens. It would likely require changes to current eligibility criteria, which already have various residency and immigration status requirements. The bill represents a significant shift in who can access this core welfare benefit.

This bill removes the 'two-child limit' rule in Universal Credit (a payment for people on low incomes). Currently, families only get extra money for their first two children; this bill would mean families get the same extra payment for all their children, potentially helping larger families have more money for essentials.

This bill changes how Universal Credit (the main welfare benefit for working-age people) is calculated for care leavers, young people who have left the local authority care system. Currently, care leavers aged 18-21 receive a reduced standard allowance (the basic monthly payment). The bill would entitle care leavers to receive the full standard allowance available to other adults, recognizing that they typically lack family financial support that other young people might have. This aims to reduce poverty and improve financial stability for one of the most vulnerable groups in the UK.

This bill aims to stop people on zero hours contracts from being 'sanctioned' (having their Universal Credit payments reduced or stopped) when they can't meet work-search requirements due to their unpredictable, irregular working hours. It recognizes that zero hours workers face unique challenges because their employer doesn't guarantee them any set hours of work.

This bill aims to stop the government from penalizing (sanctioning) people who receive Universal Credit and work on zero hours contracts. Zero hours contracts mean workers have no guaranteed hours, so the bill argues these people shouldn't be punished for not meeting strict job-seeking rules when their work is so unpredictable.

This bill would expand 'universal jurisdiction' - giving UK courts the ability to prosecute serious international crimes (like war crimes or torture) that happen anywhere in the world. Currently, these powers are limited, so this bill would make them broader.

This bill enables local authorities and community groups to temporarily use vacant commercial properties (such as empty shops or offices) without needing the owner's permission, provided certain conditions are met. It aims to prevent urban decay, reduce blight caused by long-term empty properties, and activate unused spaces for community benefit, such as pop-up shops, cultural events, or social enterprises. The bill creates a legal framework allowing temporary occupation for a defined period, after which the property must be returned to the owner. It balances the interests of property owners with community needs and local economic vitality.

This bill reviews and potentially reforms the Vaccine Damage Payments Act, which provides compensation to people who suffer severe adverse reactions to vaccines. The current scheme pays a one-off lump sum of £120,000 to those who can prove they've been significantly disabled by a vaccine. The bill would examine whether this Act needs updating, including whether payment levels are adequate, eligibility criteria are fair, and processes are accessible, given changes in medical knowledge and vaccination programmes since the Act was established in 1979.

This bill strengthens the legal framework around vehicle registration marks (number plates) in the UK, creating new criminal offences and penalties for misusing, altering, or obscuring registration marks. The legislation targets activities like displaying fake plates, deliberately obscuring characters to evade traffic enforcement cameras, and using registration marks fraudulently. It aims to close legal gaps and increase penalties to deter these offences, which are often linked to more serious crimes including vehicle theft, fly-tipping, and evading tolls or traffic fines.

This bill updates UK laws to allow new vehicle and aircraft technologies to be developed and used. It covers things like self-driving cars, electric vehicles, and aviation innovations, giving the government power to set safety rules and standards for these new technologies.

This bill proposes giving special consideration to ex-military personnel (veterans) when they're sentenced for crimes, but only when the court decides not to send them to prison. It aims to help veterans who've served their country but have since committed offences, by recognizing their service when deciding their punishment.

This bill aims to improve how crime victims are treated by creating a Code of Practice - a set of official rules and standards that public services must follow. It focuses on making sure victims receive proper support, information, and respect as they go through the criminal justice system.

This bill aims to give crime victims and people affected by anti-social behaviour better legal rights and clearer support from the justice system. It would set out what victims are entitled to (like updates on their case) and potentially give them more involvement in criminal proceedings.

This bill would make voting a civic duty that UK citizens must do by law, similar to systems used in some other countries like Australia. Currently, voting in the UK is voluntary - this would change that to compulsory voting in elections.

The Waste Incinerators Bill establishes new regulatory frameworks for waste incineration facilities across the UK. It sets stricter emissions standards, requires enhanced monitoring of air pollutants, and mandates improved waste-to-energy efficiency levels. The bill also introduces tighter planning controls for new incinerator sites and strengthens enforcement powers for local authorities and environmental regulators.

This bill would require the UK to set up an official register that tracks recycled waste from collection through to its final use. Essentially, it creates a record-keeping system to make sure that when we put items in recycling bins, they actually get recycled rather than being sent to landfill or shipped abroad illegally.

The Waste Tyres Bill establishes a framework for managing end-of-life tyres in the UK, placing responsibility on tyre producers and importers to finance the collection and recycling of waste tyres. The bill aims to reduce environmental harm from fly-tipping and improper disposal by creating an extended producer responsibility (EPR) scheme. It sets standards for how waste tyres must be processed, potentially creating a market for recycled tyre materials used in products like playground surfaces, road surfaces, and industrial goods.

The Water (Agricultural Pollution) Bill aims to reduce water pollution caused by farming activities, particularly from nutrient runoff (nitrogen and phosphorus), pesticides, and sediment that contaminate rivers, lakes, and groundwater. The bill introduces stricter regulations on farming practices, requiring farmers to implement measures such as buffer zones near water sources, limits on fertiliser use, and mandatory reporting of certain agricultural activities. It establishes enforcement mechanisms and potential penalties for non-compliance, while also providing funding and support to help farmers transition to more sustainable practices. The legislation targets improving water quality across England while balancing the needs of the agricultural sector.

This bill requires water companies in England and Wales to provide special reduced-price water tariffs (cheaper bills) for people who cannot afford normal charges. It aims to ensure vulnerable people can still access clean water without facing financial hardship.

The Welfare Reform Act 2007 changed how the UK welfare system works by placing more emphasis on helping people find employment rather than just providing long-term benefits. It introduced new requirements for people receiving benefits and created support programs to help them train and get jobs.

This bill would require the UK government to think about the long-term wellbeing of future generations when making important decisions. It aims to make sure that today's choices on issues like climate change, health, and resources don't harm people who will live in Britain decades from now.

This bill would require the government and public bodies to think about how their decisions today will affect people in the future. It aims to stop short-term thinking that creates long-term problems, like ignoring climate change, pollution, or spending all the money now and leaving debt for later.

This bill would require the UK government to think about how its policies affect future generations' wellbeing. It would make politicians consider long-term consequences on areas like climate change, public health, and living standards before making important decisions, rather than just focusing on immediate problems.

This bill requires the government to think about how its decisions today will affect people in the future, like on climate change, natural resources, and public health. It's designed to make sure that policies don't just focus on short-term benefits but also protect the wellbeing of generations to come.

This bill aims to make the government think about long-term consequences before making major decisions. It would require lawmakers to assess how policies on things like climate, jobs, and health will impact people in 10, 20, or 50 years' time, rather than just focusing on immediate results.

This Act allows the government to spend money on a compensation scheme for Windrush generation members - people who arrived in the UK legally but were wrongly treated as illegal immigrants, losing jobs and homes. It aims to pay them money to repair the harm caused by government mistakes.

This bill aims to make sure people who don't have a gas connection (and so can't get the standard Winter Fuel Allowance) can still claim money to help pay for heating their homes during winter. Currently, the allowance is mainly designed for gas-heated homes, leaving some people without this support.

This bill asks Parliament to approve giving the Prime Minister the legal power to trigger Article 50 of the EU treaty, which formally starts the process of the UK leaving the European Union. It's a straightforward yes-or-no vote on whether the government can proceed with Brexit negotiations.

This bill aims to make sure women are included in peace talks and protected from harm during armed conflicts and wars. It would require the UK government to create plans that give women a proper role in decision-making about peace, and to work towards stopping violence against women in conflict zones worldwide.

The Women, Peace and Security Bill requires the UK government to develop and implement a comprehensive national action plan addressing women's roles in conflict prevention, peacebuilding, and post-conflict reconstruction. It establishes legal obligations for government departments to consider gender equality and women's participation in peace processes, conflict resolution, and security policy. The bill aims to increase women's representation in peace negotiations, security institutions, and decision-making roles that affect conflict-affected communities. It also requires the government to report regularly to Parliament on progress in achieving these objectives.

This bill aims to give more people, especially those in flexible or gig economy jobs, legal protection as 'workers' rather than self-employed. It would extend rights like the minimum wage and paid leave to more people, while clarifying exactly who the law protects.

This Act aims to give workers more predictable working hours and clearer employment terms. It requires employers to provide workers with better notice of their shifts and more stable contracts, especially for those currently on zero-hours or unpredictable arrangements.

This bill changes how the law defines who counts as a 'worker' and what rights they have. It aims to give more employment protections to people in non-traditional jobs (like delivery drivers or freelancers), rather than just those with traditional employment contracts.

This bill would make parents legally responsible for crimes committed by their children, potentially through fines or court-ordered parenting programmes. The aim is to use parental accountability as a way to prevent youth crime and encourage parents to supervise their children more closely.

This bill establishes a Youth Mobility Scheme that allows young people from EU countries to live and work in the UK for an extended period, and reciprocally allows young UK citizens to do the same in EU member states. The scheme replaces the freedom of movement that ended with Brexit, creating a bilateral agreement framework between the UK and participating EU countries. It aims to facilitate cultural exchange, work experience, and travel opportunities for young adults typically aged 18-35. The bill sets out the legal basis for visa-free or visa-simplified entry, work rights, and residency conditions under this new arrangement.

The Youth Services Bill establishes a framework for funding, delivering, and regulating youth services across the UK. It aims to improve access to youth clubs, mentoring programmes, and recreational activities for young people aged 11-19. The bill sets minimum service standards that councils must meet and creates accountability mechanisms to ensure consistent quality. It also introduces grants and incentives for voluntary organisations to expand their youth provision.

This bill aims to ensure that Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) standards and regulations accommodate a wider range of body shapes, sizes, and characteristics across the UK population. Currently, many PPE standards are based on limited anthropometric data that may not fit people of different ethnicities, women, people with disabilities, and those outside average sizing ranges. The bill would require manufacturers and regulators to develop and test PPE using more inclusive sizing and design standards, ensuring that workers in high-risk industries (such as healthcare, construction, and emergency services) can access properly fitting protective equipment.
